Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour (Mr,. Gordon). I am informed that in certain municipalities in my county instructions have been given to reduce the rates of direct relief, and it is reported also that these instructions were

Apple Shipments
issued by the federal government. Will the minister inform the house upon whose authority the rates for direct relief are fixed and if the federal government has issued instructions that these rates shall be reduced in the province of Quebec?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was good enough to direct my attention to the questions he proposed to ask. In reply to the first two questions I would say that in the case of his district or any other district in the province of Quebec or elsewhere in Canada no instructions have been issued by the federal government to reduce the amount of direct relief to be granted to those in need. The only conditions which this government has at any time laid down with respect to direct relief have been to define direct relief as consisting of food, fuel, clothing and shelter or the equivalent thereof, and that there shall be no discrimination in the granting of relief to any applicant by reason of political, racial, religious or other considerations. No limit has ever been set by this government to the amount of relief which shall be granted to any applicant, this being constitutionally a matter wholly within the determination and judgment of the local authorities. It will also be obvious to members of the house that, even aside from the constitutional aspect, such matters are properly for the local authorities to determine.
Answering my hon. friend's third question, "On whose authority rates for direct relief axe fixed?" I would say that municipalities must determine, first, whether relief shall be granted and, second, to whom and in what amount it shall be granted. I also presume that such decisions on the part of municipalities receive provincial approval. As a matter of fact I am informed and understand that in Quebec the provincial govemmtemt determines the amount which may be expended in each municipality on direct relief.
Answering -the hon. member's last question, "Has the federal government issued instructions in the province of Quebec to reduce the amount of relief?" The answer is no. This government has been most careful never to invade in any manner the jurisdiction of either the provincial or municipal authorities either in our relief legislation or in the administration thereof.

I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Agriculture. In view of newspaper statements in Nova Scotia to the effect that the British Ministry of Agriculture has no alarm about the pest known as the apple maggot, and in view of the fact that these statements may have created a wrong impression calculated to lead to efforts being relaxed in the extermination of this pest, will the minister state whether all danger of an embargo on the entry of Canadian apples into Great Britain is past?

The hon. member for Hants-Kings gave notice that he was going to ask this question. It is very important that attention should be called to this matter. The apple maggot is quite common in a number of provinces in Canada. When the Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries of the United Kingdom instructed Mr. Fryer to investigate the possibility of the Colorado beetle being imported into the old country if importation of potatoes were allowed, he also instructed him to go very carefully into the danger of the importation of the apple maggot in infested apples.
So far as the shipping of the 1932 crop of apples is concerned, due to the very close supervision of the fruit inspectors with the cooperation of the shippers in the applegrowing provinces, only one shipment consisting of about twelve barrels of infested apples has gone into the United Kingdom. It was learned that a number of barrels of infested apples were on the boat and every effort was made to catch those and have them removed before the boat left, but in the cargo there were some twelve barrels that were shipped to the old country.
The fact that in a letter that I put on Hansard on February 10 last, the Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries referred even to this small shipment, shows the great danger of an embargo being placed upon our apples if infested apples are shipped in any quantity to the United Kingdom. I do not think I can do better in this connection than read again the last paragraph of the letter of the Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries of the old land:
Mr. Fryer has also reported to me the measures which you contemplate in order to prevent the export to this country of apples infested with the apple fruit fly. Much to our pleasure, it has not so far been necessary for us to place any restrictions on apples imported from the dominion. The discovery of an infested consignment last October-
That is the one to which reference has been made.
-was, we hope, only an isolated case; and after considering Mr. Fryer's account of the steps you are taking, I have decided that it

The hon. member for Skeena was
good enough to intimate to me his intention of asking this question. On February 1, 1933, employees in the mine, smelter, coke ovens and shops ceased work, demanding increases in wages and reductions in rates for board and rent. From 800 to 1,000 workers are reported to be involved, from 400 to 500 having joined the Mine Workers' Union of Canada, affiliated with the Workers' Unity League.
It is not clear whether the other employees are on strike or merely deterred by pickets from working. A report from the union states that wages were as low as $2.75 a day, and an increase of fifty cents per day was desired ; that board was $1.10 per day and rent for a shack six by ten feet 16 per month. A decrease of twenty per cent in board and rent was demanded. Recognition of the union was also demanded.
It is reported in the press that a clash between the provincial police and the strikers

Second Narrows Bridge
occurred on February 4, and that several were injured and in hospital, while eight had been arrested.
The plant was closed down on February 4, and the company is reported to have stated that it had been operated at a loss for some time and would be closed permanently if the strike continued for any length of time. Hon. members will understand that this is a base metal mine, and of course the product from the mine is selling at a very low price at the present time, so much so that I have no doubt that not only this base metal mine but probably all others with very few exceptions on this continent are having a most difficult struggle to keep their plants operating.
On February 9 a dispatch from Victoria stated that 310 of the strikers had voted to return to work and that the company expected the dispute would terminate within a few days.
The men have not made any application to the department to intercede, so far as I am aware, unless it has come in to-day. If such an application is made the department will, of course, exercise what authority it has and do anything possible in order to bring about a satisfactory solution of the alleged trouble.

On behalf of the people of North Vancouver and Greater Vancouver who are very anxious to have repairs made to the second narrows bridge and cannot understand why there has been so much delay, I would ask the Prime Minister if he can give us any idea when the repairs will be started.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it must be within the
knowledge of the hon. gentleman that when this parliament was asked to reenact certain legislation and amend the then existing legislation with respect to the second narrows bridge, which, if I remember aright, had been destroyed in part and with respect to which destruction it was held that there was liability against the company, we were told by those who had the matter in hand, the undertaking being owned by corporations and municipalities, that nothing further was required. This government was told that distinctly and positively. Later it was sought to obtain assistance from the government for the construction of the bridge because the methods to which resort was had, had failed. Then the government discovered that a receiver had been appointed and that a contract was outstanding, 53719-136
and it was asked that the government should take over the contract; that is, afford the means for providing for the payment of the obligations under the contract.
The bridge involves the construction of a substructure and a superstructure. The construction of the substructure being under water, with a swift current flowing, is a matter of very great importance, and in order that the foundation might be properly determined it was necessary that divers should inspect the bottom of the stream and that borings should be made. As a result of all the representations that were made, the government took steps to enable the Vancouver harbour commissioners to take over the undertaking, but when the undertaking was taken over it was found that there were outstanding contracts which had not been let by tender, and that the bridge was to be constructed by arrangement between one producer of material and bridge-builder and the corporation. The contract, it is true, is approved by the court, but in consequence of representations that were made to the government from Vancouver itself that it was undesirable in the public interest that an undertaking of this character should be built without tenders being called, the government then instructed the harbour commissioners to ascertain what could be done in the way of having tenders called. It was then represented that it would take a very long time to prepare the plans for the superstructure as well as to determine with exactitude what would have to be done with respect to the substructure.
Be that as it may, the government determined that no opportunity should be given to those who were seeking so strongly to obtain their assistance, later to charge that the government had been a party to the letting of contracts without tenders, and accordingly instructions were given that steps be taken to prepare proper plans and specifications for the purpose of enabling tenders to be called for the construction of both the superstructure and the substructure. That we are told involves delay, but the delay is not the delay of this government. It is the delay of those who had control of the enterprise from the start, but who did not desire any assistance from us until later, and then when assistance was sought we were confronted with contracts which involved the expenditure of moneys to be found by this government for the purpose of constructing without tenders a work that would cost a large sum of money.
At the moment negotiations are pending, I am informed, between the constituted

C.NJi.-Annual Report

authority of the harbour and the bridge company for the acquisition of the plans prepared by the bridge company, and not by the public authority, to enable tenders to be called. Yesterday a telegram came indicating that possibly with the aid of another consulting engineer the plans might be much more rapidly prepared than was at first thought.
I may add that Mr. Monsarrat, one of the most eminent engineers in Canada, has been out upon the ground and has gone over the undertaking with great care and made a report, and intimated that if the present plans prepared by a private company are to be used for the purpose of constructing the bridge, much money will have to be paid for them and there might be difficulties in connection with other companies tendering on plans prepared by a rival or competing company.
I know of few matters which I have had occasion to investigate in which you find so many cross-currents of interest and of influence, and in the end we determined that there should be no opportunity given to say that the public moneys under the control of the harbour authority had been expended otherwise than through tenders being awarded to those who were able to build the work for the least money having regard to their fitness to undertake it.

speechtext:
Mr. S. C. ROBINSON (West Essex) moved the second reading of Bill No. 14, to amend the Export Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving the second reading of the amendment to the Export Act passed in 1930 it is not my intention to go over the ground I covered on March 24, 1930, and on May 18, 1931. At the time the amendment was passed in 1930 I think hon. members on this and on the other side of the house were of the opinion that we were going to get something in return from the United States for our friendly gesture. As everyone knows we have received nothing. First there was the Hawley-Smoot tariff which was so disastrous to the farmers of this country. Secondly there were amendments to the Immigration Act which affected the commuters, and especially those living at border points. In 1927 over 15,000 people, working in Detriot and suburbs, were living in the border cities. A great many of them were Americans. Since that time the number has been reduced to between 1,000 and 1,500. Not only that, but Canadians working in Detroit or Americans residing in Windsor

Liquor Export-Mr. Robinson
were forced to move to Detroit to carry on their work in that city.
Restrictions are not the same on this side of the line. Americans are free to come and go as they please, and they hold high positions in the larger industries of the border cities. A great many Americans with whom I have talked have stated that in cutting off the export of good liquor and forcing the American people to buy moonshine and other concoctions Canada has been guilty of an unfriendly act towards her neighbour. There was never a better opportunity than that presented in 1930, at the time the restrictions were enforced, to make an arrangement with the United States whereby commuters on both sides of the line would be free to come and go as they pleased, as they had done until recent years.
The situation concerning exports of liquor differs greatly from that which obtained two years ago. The first cause of the change may be traced to the depressed conditions, and the second to the result of the United States election which took place on November 8, 1932. While some years ago the state of Michigan passed a prohibition act by an overwhelming majority, in the election held last fall prohibition legislation was defeated by a three to one vote. There can be no argument that Canada needs revenue. Probably I would do well at this time to place on Hansard figures showing our exports of whisky, spirits and beer for the year ending March 31, 1930, the last figures obtainable from the bureau of statistics, and the loss in revenue suffered by Canada as a result of the amendment to the Export Act:

The worst feature since this act went into force is that of the smuggling of alcohol into Canada which has increased by leaps and bounds. No service knows better what that amounts to than the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I have here an extract from a report of Sir Henry Drayton, chairman of the liquor control board of the province of Ontario, for the year ending October 31, 1931. It says:
The smuggling of spurious liquor into Ontario, from the prohibited areas of the United States, at the first impression appears well nigh incredible. The reports, however, of commissions and inquiries, governnienitally constituted in the United States, establish, without doubt, that spurious liquor and alcohol are largely trafficked in that country. Further, spurious liquors can be manufactured very cheaply. The usual base is alcohol; sometimes pure, sometimes absolutely poisonous. The added water, colouring matter and flavouring cost but little. Sixty-five per cent over-proof alcohol can be readily produced for forty-five cents a gallon, but the dominion excise tax alone amounts to $14.85 a gallon. American alcohol pays no taxes and has been sold in Ontario as low as $3 a gallon.

The Toronto Telegram of November 19, 1932, said:
Most Canadians felt that Premier King had gone beyond the requirements of international courtesy in complying with the request to place a ban on the export of intoxicants. Canada
had no wish to interfere in the policy of the United States on the wet-dry question but it was felt that the Prime Minister of that day was asking too much when he called upon the taxpayers of Canada to spend $15,000,000 in helping to enforce the laws of another country. Liquor export, after all, was a legitimate enterprise so far as this country was concerned.
Here is one from the Monetary Times, Toronto, of February 12, 1932:
In the year ending March 31, 1931, we sent some 2,000,000 gallons of whiskey to the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon, practically all of which was reshipped to the United States. We lost the excise tax of $9 per gallon and then had the trouble of seeing that the goods actually went to their destination. It was a beautiful gesture on the part of our previous government, blit it was of little value; for the thirsty American is still slaking his parched tongue and doing it more cheaply than before. From a sentimental standpoint it was supposed to earn us the undying gratitude of all our cousins to the south, but we find that many of our neighbours in the northern states are wet anyway while those in the dry regions are too far away to be affected.
May we repeat that the morals of the liquor business have nothing to do with the case. Any visitor to an American city can see, if he wishes, that the Volstead Act is as often honoured in the breach as otherwise. Spirituous liquors are^ being drunk and we are losing the revenue with no compensating benefit. The national strong-box in its present condition would be greatly helped by it.
Here is another, from the Financial Times of Montreal, dated November 18, 1932:
Though passed by an overwhelming house majority in 1930, the liquor export ban was never demanded by any substantial nation-wide body of opinion. In Ontario there was an outcry against the short-circuiting of supposed liquor exports but the provincial government effectively squashed that end of the bootlegging trade. In the face of these considerations, it

Liquor Export-Mr. Robinson
may be asked: why was the law passed? The answer is that the law was one of those moves which few politicians actively support but which few dare openly oppose.
This is from the Montreal Gazette of December 10, 1932:
In pursuance of its policy of good will to the United States, at whatever cost to the Canadian people, the King government, in 1930, induced parliament to amend the Export Act to prohibit the granting of clearances to vessels carrying Canadian liquor to countries wherein the sale of such liquor was illegal. The amendment, though general in its terms, was designed admittedly to help the United States whose efforts at enforcing the prohibition law had failed. Parliament passed the amendment against its better judgment, the then opposition being unwilling to give the government the political advantage which, it was thought, might result from a division. It was an interesting exhibition of legislation based upon expediency rather than upon conviction.
The Border Cities Star of December 9, 1932, has this to say:
Public opinion on this subject has undergone a radical change. Public opinion favoured stopping export. But the public understood that Canada was going to get some worthwhile concession from the United States in return for this important favour. Canada got nothing. Consequently there is no longer much disposition here to assist the United States in the enforcement of its dry laws-particularly in view of the fact that the American voters have vigorously repudiated these laws themselves.
Here is one from the Ottawa Journal of February 2, 1933, headed:
May as Well Use the Front Door
Because, actually, all that the 1930 legislation did was to send our liquor to the United States by a more circuitous route. By the back door instead of the front door.
Last year our liquor exports to St. Pierre and Miquelon, which have a few hundred inhabitants, were 1,616,177 gallons. The liquor went to the United States.
We shipped 134,000 gallons to Bermuda; 106,000 gallons to British Honduras; 117,000 gallons to the West Indies. Most of this was for the United States.
We shipped 252,000 gallons to French Oceania, in the Pacific; and most of this went to the United States. French Oceania never bought a gallon of liquor from us until after the 1930 legislation.
In the circumstances, the 1930 law, under which we are supposed to protect good (but sometimes thirsty) Americans from our own sumptuary habits, seems to be little more than a nice bit of make-believe, or hypocrisy. And the worst of it is, it is costing us a lot of money.
Now I quote from the Border Cities Star of November 10, 1932:
Everyone seemed to take it for granted, at the time, that Mr. King had a formal agreement or at least a gentleman's understanding with the government at Washington by which this country would receive a substantial concession from the United States in return for

the favour we were doing Uncle Sam by cutting off the business of Canadian liquor exporters. No announcement along these lines was made, but most persons concluded that the lack of announcement was merely a matter^ of diplomatic policy, Washington, for domestic political purposes, not caring to reveal that concessions had been made to Canada. However, as we mentioned before, time passed and the cold truth finally came home to us all-the government had given everything and received nothing. We had something substantial to "trade" and we muffed the opportunity. .

speechtext: May I ask from what my hon. friend is reading?

I am reading from an editorial appearing in the Border Cities Star of November 10, 1932.
Then and there, of course, enthusiasm for the ban on export started to wither and decay. And the withering and decaying process was intensified as politicians and officials in Washington continued to jack up the_ American tariff against our country and to devise further ways and means for keeping Canadians from crossing the boundary line in quest of employment or even, in some cases, for purely social purposes. Our people came to the bitter conclusion that they had been "let down" by their own leaders, that Mr. King and his associates had simply "missed the boat" in dealing with the boys at Washington.	_
A plebiscite on the question to-day would give Colonel Robinson a resounding majority for his proposal to end the export ban. No one familiar with public sentiment can doubt this. In addition, as we have said, the United States has "gone off the dry standard," thus destroying even anything in the shape of a moral argument, real or fancied, against the export of alcoholic beverages from Canada to that country.
Now I quote from the St. Thomas Times-Journal of November 16, 1932:
What has been the result? There has been no let-up in liquor violations in the United States. Liquor, good and bad, but mostly bad, flows more freely than ever in the "land of the free." And the reciprocal concessions, where are they? Nowhere. In place of them the United States has built higher tariff walls against our goods; tightened up its immigration laws to keep out Canadian labour and to prevent Canadians taking up residence there. Canada's gesture-well-meaning though it may have been-cost the dominion $15,000,000 a year in revenue, without our getting a single thing in return.
I quote now from the Montreal Gazette of February 1, 1933:
Since the November election in the United States, with its overwhelming repudiation of the eighteenth amendment and the v olstead law, the Canadian liquor embargo cannot be defended upon the pretence of cooperating to uphold the policy of a friendly country. Since the United States is no longer in favour of prohibition- if, indeed, it ever was-there oan be no reason in the world for withholding one of the few export commodities which finds a ready market in that country. Moreover, the

Liquor Export-Mr. Mackenzie King
Ottawa treasury stands in the utmost need of any and every increase in revenue that can be legitimately provided. As the Prime Minister has stated, and as every thoughtful citizen knows, Canada is dangerously near the limit of its capacity to pay taxes. By legalizing the export of liquor, however, a former source of income can be reopened without hardship to the public and to the advantage of an important industry. In these circumstances the embargo should be removed, and the sooner the better.
I hold in my hand a map of the city of Washington, which appeared in the Border Cities Star of February 18, 1932. Shown on this map are dots representing speakeasies which have been raided by the police, totalling 1,155 and of these three were located on government property close to the capitol.
I believe this is all I have to say at this time, Mr. Speaker. In my mind, and in the minds of those who have the interests of the country at heart, the repeal of this act will benefit this country in many ways. It will help labour; it will result in the purchase of supplies and material, and will aid the distilling and brewing industries. I hope this measure will receive the favourable consideration of the house.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROPOSED REPEAL OF PROHIBITION OF LIQUOR EXPORT, ENACTED IN 1930
speechtext:
So far as I have heard, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Robinson), and who is the mover of this resolution, has not given a single reason why the legislation passed in 1930 should be repealed at the present time, if I confine that remark to arguments that really bear upon the essential features of the measure and the reason for its adoption in 1930.
My hon. friend spoke at some length about some quid pro quo which we should have received from the United States because of the passage of this measure. I never heard or thought of any such quid pro quo at the time or at any time. I do not think the bill was passed with any expectation that it would lead to other measures on the part of the United States. The bill was passed in the interests of Canada itself, in order .to maintain respect for our own laws and to fulfil our treaty obligations. While no doubt the legislation was of assistance to the United States, it was not a measure that had relation primarily to the United States; its primary relation was to Canada, to fulfilling our own obligations, maintaining the integrity of our own public services, and seeing to it that our own citizens, and particularly our own officials, did not become allied with smugglers and criminal gangsters in their efforts to violate the laws of another country.
This is 1933; it is three years since the bill which it is now sought to repeal passed the house, and I might remind hon. members that when the measure was adopted it passed both the house and the Senate without division, as I recall it. I do not know what circumstances have arisen in the interval which should cause the parliament of Canada to change its mind with regard to the purpose it was hoped would be fulfilled by the enactment of this legislation.

speechtext:
I am glad to be corrected if that is so. The vote against the measure was so small that I had forgotten it. Perhaps, I cannot do better than state to the house, in the terms of the explanatory note which accompanies the bill, the objects which according to that statement are sought to be effected. The explanation reads:
The object of this bill is, by repealing the above section, ito restore to the revenues of Canada the large amount of revenue lost by its enactment, and to open the way by international treaty or convention for reciprocal duties and obligations on the part of the two governments concerned. It is also an effort to help the serious unemployment situation in Canada, and to assist in the prevention of smuggling.
There are four alleged reasons given, and I shall deal with each in turn, taking the last first. It is stated that the enactment of this bill is to assist in the prevention of smuggling. My hon. friend seeks to repeal a section of an act which was passed for the purpose of assisting in the suppression of smuggling by a bill which he says is to assist in the suppression of smuggling. I fail to see how he can claim that the suppression of smuggling will be one of the effects of his measure. I regard his bill rather as a measure to assist smuggling.
I should like to point out how the law as it formerly stood aided smuggling and how smuggling will be again aided if the amendment passed in 1930 is repealed. Not only was smuggling aided, but it was aided at the instance of the government of Canada and with the direct assistance of government officials. I should like my hon. friend to realize that from my point of view that is the most serious objection to be made to his measure, apart from its violation of the principle on which the original measure is based. If the amendment of 1930 is repealed we will again (have the government of Canada,
2160	COMMONS
Liquor Export-Mr. Mackenzie Kino
through its officials, knowingly and openly aiding and abetting smuggling in the violation of the laws of a neighbouring and friendly country. What was the procedure before and what will it be again if the amendment proposed by my hon. friend is adopted?
In the first place, in order to take out liquor from a warehouse os' distillery for export it had to be entered for purposes of duty. If the liquor was going to a foreign country which did not prohibit the importation of liquor, no duty was paid but a bond amounting to twice the amount of the excise was exacted. When the Department of National Revenue received a certificate to the effect that the liquor had been successfully landed in that country, the bond was cancelled. In the case of the United States, which prohibited the importation of liquor, that process, namely the taking of a bond prior to export could not be followed by the department, so the department adopted the plan of requiring those who desired to ship liquor to the United States to paj7 on liquor so exported an amount equivalent to the excise duty.
My hon. friend says that his measure is intended for purposes of revenue, and I should like to show how this revenue would be collected. The duty would be paid at the time the liquor was taken out of the warehouse or distillery and whoever was shipping the liquor would have to state that it was going to the United States. The liquor would be entered in the books of the government of Canada as going to the United States, a country known to prohibit the importation of liquor and the customs officials would be obliged to make that entry knowing that they were assisting those who were desirous of smuggling and violating the laws of another country. That is the first step.
After the liquor had been entered in that manner, government assistance would be still necessary to get the liquor from the warehouse, brewery or distillery to the dock from which it was to clear for the United States. This step would be impossible without some cooperation upon the part of the officials of the Department of National Revenue. This cooperation would consist of giving a permit for the transportation of the liquor from the warehouse to the port from which it was to be cleared for the United States, and the permit would bear upon its face the statement that the liquor was going to the United States. Everyone having to do with the handling of that liquor, whether customs officials, train 'employees or others would know that that liquor was to be smuggled into the United States, they would all become 
parties to the smuggling. After the liquor, by virtue of this permit which had been granted by government officials or by the government of Canada-for after all it is the government; the government is responsible for the acts of its officials-had been transported from the distillery to the end of steel, it would have to be put on board a vessel for the United States. Before this vessel could be cleared for the United States another customs official would have to go on board to make sure, by examining the permit, that the liquor on board that vessel was the liquor that came from the distillery, that it had paid the excise duty and Was going to the United States.

speechtext: That is not required for vessels of five tons and under.

subtopic: PROPOSED REPEAL OF PROHIBITION OF LIQUOR EXPORT, ENACTED IN 1930
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend will find that the vessels which would be engaged in rum running would require clearances.
A olearance would have to be obtained and I would point out that that clearance would have to be given by a government official. The olearance would state that the vessel had on board liquor destined for the United States notwithstanding it was known that liquor could not be lawfully imported into the United States. When a vessel known to everyone to be in the hands of rum runnere was thus cleared, it would be cleared by virtue of the authority of the government of Canada.
This is something which any country which has regard for its own laws and the integrity and probity of its own officials cannot afford to countenance for one moment. The feeling I had when I presented the amendment to the act was that this procedure not only was demoralizing as regards encouraging the practice of rum running, but that it was particularly demoralizing to the whole customs service of Canada. Our customs service is intended to safeguard the revenues of the country and to prevent anything in the nature of smuggling. We cannot expect it to be an honest service if its officials are expected knowingly to assist smuggling operations.
Another extraordinary thing in connection, with this whole business was the fact that at the time the excise duty was paid on liqour to be smuggled into the United States, not only were the officials of the federal government at Ottawa made aware of that fact but also the officials of the provincial government at Toronto. The control of the sale of liquor is a state monopoly in the province of Ontario, and it was alleged that- the giving of such information to the provincial authorities would!

Liquor Export-Mr. Mackenzie King
effectively safeguard against the liquor being taken off the trains and short circuited back into Ontario before being sent across the border. In other words, the officials of the Ontario liquor control department were expected to assume the attitude that by making sure that the laws of the United States were violated they would thereby be ensuring that the laws of the province of Ontario were not violated. I submit that as members of parliament we are here as law makers, and not as law breakers, or to assist in the breaking of the laws of our own or any other country. So far as the government officials are concerned, they are in a very difficult position; no matter what the conscience of an official may be, he is supposedly bound to carry out the instructions given to him by his superior officer. The only defence which it is possible for officials to make in performing duties of this bind in the light of the knowledge they have of existing conditions is that their business is simply to collect or to protect the revenue and nothing more. But, as I say, when they know that the effect of their action goes very much further than the collection of revenue; that it is a matter not merely of collecting revenue but of getting such revenue as can be secured, by becoming accomplices of rum runners and gangsters, a government that is responsible for placing on its officials an obligation of that kind, is assuming a very grave responsibility. That is the first objection I take to the bill of my hon. friend from West Essex. It is in the nature, not of a measure to help in the suppression of rum running, but rather of a measure to assist, and encourage rum running and the violation of the laws of another country. It makes of government officials a link between those who wish to make money by violating the laws of another country, and the bootleggers, rum runners and criminal gangsters who operate from a like aim.
The hon. member supported his bill by saying that this legislation will help to give revenue, and also that it will help to give employment. If we are reduced in this country to the position where the state can get its revenues and provide employment only by becoming partners in the rum running business, matters have come to a very strange pass. The less my hon. friend says about our attempting to get revenue in that way, and the less he tries to defend such action in the parliament of this country, the wiser he will be. I submit that anything of the kind is encouraging lawlessness generally; it is putting a premium on the direct violation of a country's laws. The hon. member must
surely have forgotten the condition we had along the southwest-Ontario frontier three years ago as a result of the bootlegging and rum running business, and the extent to which it was being carried on there. That part of our country was becoming a base for criminal operations, and criminal operations not confined to the business merely of rum running. We were getting into Canada professional gangsters in very considerable numbers, whose activities were finding expression in a number of directions. Having gotten successfully away from that state of affairs, we had better not seek to return to it by any measure that will have any such effect. If my hon. friend's bill were to be adopted and this parliament were to repeal the enactment of 1930, the effect would be that on the day after the repeal we should witness in and about the vicinity of the community in which my hon. friend lives, the reassembling of those classes of persons in large numbers, and heaven alone knows, with conditions what they are at present in different parts of this continent, what might result from such an association.
Let me mention the other factor that is set forth as a reason for passing this amendment:
To open a way by international treaty or convention for reciprocal duties and obligations on the part of the two governments concerned
I am afraid my hon. friend is not aware of the treaties that already bind us in the matter of assistance in the suppression of smuggling. This is not opening a way; it is destroying a way already provided. It is violating absolutely more than one treaty obligation. If this amendment should become law, we would be violating treaty obligations of the most important character.

More particularly, the different parts of the British Empire that became parties to the convention undertook to assist in connection with the laws of the United States regarding alcoholic beverages.

That its provisions related to importations from the sea, and the nature of the agreement was amongst other things to extend the right of search to vessels that were believed to have liquor on board, from the three mile limit to a distance that would be equivalent to one hour's steaming from shore.

speechtext: I am not criticizing the right hon. gentleman's argument, and I do not say I am not in sympathy with it, but if it is sound, why do the British crown colonies, such as the West Indies-I am not talking of the dominions-still allow clearances to the United States?

subtopic: PROPOSED REPEAL OF PROHIBITION OF LIQUOR EXPORT, ENACTED IN 1930
speechtext: The crown colonies will have to answer for themselves. It is our duty as members of the Canadian parliament to answer for ourselves, and we in this parliament, both the House of Commons and the Senate, have approved that treaty. Both houses of parliament have approved a treaty which was expressly entered into in 1924 in the first instance by the British government, for the reason that the parties thereto were desirous of avoiding any difficulties which might arise between them in connection with the laws of the United States regarding alcoholic beverages. If differences were likely to arise on the high seas, I submit they are as nothing compared with those that are likely to arise where there are frontiers as immediate as the one between Canada and the United States, and where smuggling takes place not merely across the high seas but across river channels that are far from being wide. The reasons for that treaty are just as strong to-day as they were when it was entered into. I remember, when the matter came up before, mentioning how the late Lord Curzon, who at the time was Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs in Great Britain, had pointed out, as the ground on which the convention should be entered into, that no country could afford to be indifferent to the domestic legislation of another country, that it was bound to have respect for its policies and the sentiment of its people, that it could not do otherwise and hope to maintain friendly relations with that other country. That is the principle I wish now to reaffirm and assert.

subtopic: PROPOSED REPEAL OF PROHIBITION OF LIQUOR EXPORT, ENACTED IN 1930
speechtext: What date was that?

subtopic: PROPOSED REPEAL OF PROHIBITION OF LIQUOR EXPORT, ENACTED IN 1930
speechtext:
That convention was ratified in Washington on January 23, 1924. Ratifications were exchanged on May

22, 1924. The convention was approved by the House of Commons of Canada on March 21, 1924, and by the Senate of Canada on April 4, 1924.
As I was saying, the point that was stressed at the time and that in the main accounted for the action of the British government, was the recognition of the fact that where a country, for reasons of its own, enacts legislation which governs its entire people, it is not the business of another country to inquire whether the legislation is wise, whether it is being enforced or not; it is its business to inquire to what extent its own citizens axe respecting their obligations not to attempt to violate the laws of another country. Lord Curzon took very strongly the position that unless that position were maintained, if shipping or commercial interests in one state sought to further their business by running counter to the legislation and practice of another state, 'as, for example, by violating the laws of another country, "a very delicate and disagreeable situation would be produced" -ithat, I think, was the phrase he used

with which it would be extremely difficult for the country whose shipping was responsible for the violation of the laws of the other country to deal. I remember at the time of introducing the legislation of 1930, having then the responsibility of Minister of External Affairs, I felt, and had reason to feel, there was possibility of serious difficulty arising any day between this country and the United States by what might take place in connection with smuggling going on between the two countries. I felt that the really grave factor that would grow' out of the situation was not one so much pertaining to the individuals participating in the traffic, as the responsibility of the government of Canada itself for their illegal action, seeing that their illegal action could not possibly have been taken except for the government itself through its officials being a party to it.
So much for the convention between Britain and the United States which we approved and to which we are parties. In 1924 the government of Canada entered into a treaty of its own with the United States for the purpose of aiding in the suppression of smuggling between the two countries. My hon. friend and colleague, the member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) was Minister of Justice at the time, and he is one of the signatories to that treaty. The treaty was approved by this parliament. Its object, as I have said, was to aid in the suppression of smuggling. Now if we amend the statute which has been enacted with the express pur-

Liquor Export-Mr. Mackenzie King
pose of suppressing smuggling by removing its effective clause we are thereby not only destroying the statute, but are absolutely violating the provisions of our own treaty with the United States.
Hon. members will recall an investigation that was made in 1926 into the administration of the customs service and the report which was presented t.o this house. That report was before the house prior to the dissolution of parliament in 1926. Hon. gentlemen opposite had a brief term of office, very brief, just prior and immediately subsequent to that dissolution, but during the time they were in office and before dissolution they introduced into this house a resolution that clearances should not be granted to vessels carrying liquor from Canada to the United States, and the resolution carried in this House of Commons. It was the resolution of hon. gentlemen opposite. They themselves supported it and were responsible for its passing through this house. That was in 1926.

subtopic: PROPOSED REPEAL OF PROHIBITION OF LIQUOR EXPORT, ENACTED IN 1930
speechtext:
In 1927 a royal commission investigated certain matters pertaining to the customs service, and again a recommendation was made that in all particulars the law should be made such that it would prevent the smuggling of liquor from Canada into the United States.
What was the position of the present prime minister and his supporters when this measure was introduced? I am perfectly frank to admit that the government of the day did not rush into action on the prohibition of liquor exports from Canada to the United States. We realized that to be at all effective any legislation would have to have back of it considerable public opinion not only as represented by hon. members in this house but throughout the country. There was doubt for a time as to whether the United States was seeking to enforce prohibition. It was not until we were perfectly sure that the government of the United States itself was doing everything in its power to enforce its own laws that we took the step which we did. But I remember very well, because I got most of the benefit of it, how my right hon. friend then leader Of the opposition waxed full of wrath against me and the government of the day for not having taken that step long before we did. That was the whole gravamen of his indictment. My right hon. friend took the view at that time, and I believe it is the view he will take to-day, having regard to his responsibility as prime minister of this country, that that step should have been taken sooner than it was. I shall be very much surprised if the prime minister to-day at the instance of any one or more of his followers reverses his own position now that he is responsible for any change in this legislation which may find its place on our statutes.
In conclusion, I should like to add that these are days when conditions are troublesome enough on this continent, and in all parts of
2164	COMMONS
Liquor Export-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
the worlds to warrant us in being a little careful about taking any step which is going to make more difficult the relations that exist between countries, particularly between countries that are immediate neighbours. We have boasted a good deal on this continent that so far as our relations with the great country to the south are concerned we of the United States and Canada have a happier way of dealing with difficulties that may arise than have any other countries in their relations with their immediate neighbours. We speak much of the settlement of our differences by means of an international joint commission to which we can point with great pride. As a consequence we are in a position on this continent to set an example to the rest of the world as to how goodwill may be maintained on both sides of an international frontier. Speaker, listening to the arguments put forward by the last speaker (Mr. Bell, Hamilton) and the hon. member for West Essex (Mr. Robinson), one would almost conclude that the estimable gentleman who was shot at recently was already seated in his place of power in the United States, and that under his supervision congress had taken action, legislation had been passed and the Volstead Act relegated to the scrap heap. As a matter of fact none of these things has yet happened. Mr. Roosevelt is still President-elect of the United States, and the Yoilstead Act is still in operation.
On second reading it is customary to discuss the principle of a bill, and at this time I wish to voice my very decided opposition to Bill No. 14, now appearing before us. I was in the house three years ago when the legislation with which this bill deals was passed, and I recall very clearly that such legislation was brought forward very, very slowly. I recall that it took several years of agitation, urging and petitioning from different public bodies, and more particularly from church bodies throughout Canada and especially throughout the province of Ontario, before this legislation was brought down. When in 1930 legislation was brought down under chapter 19 of the statutes of that year; provision was made for three points: First, that it would be unlawful to export intoxicating liquor for delivery in any country into which the importation of such liquor was prohibited by law. That condition obtained in regard to the United States at that time, and the same condition obtains to-day. The second point in the legislation was that it should be declared unlawful to grant a clearance to any vessel carrying such liquor, and the third point, that it should be declared unlawful to make any entry for exportation of such liquor. In the year 1930 that legislation was passed almost unanimously by the House of Commons. Although I have not been able to obtain the information from Hansard, owing to the in-

Liquor Export-Mr. Carmichael
ability of the Library to supply me with a copy, I believe the recorded division showed that there were only twelve or fourteen votes recorded in opposition to the legislation of that day.
Here are a few facts I would like to place before the house. Smuggling of liquor into the United States prior to 1930 was on an enormous scale. For the year ending March 31, 1926, that is four years before the legislation was passed, liquor smuggled into the United States totalled $12,572,011. For the year ending March 31, 1928, it had reached $18,380,070 an increase of almost fifty per cent. I have not got the increase for the years following that.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) says that this legislation as proposed in Bill No. 14, if enacted, would simply open the doors and start again those smuggling operations which had reached such proportions in the years prior to 1930.
On January the 8th, 9th and 10th, 1929, there was a conference held in the city of Ottawa between delegates to the number of twelve from the United States, and to the number of ten representing the Dominion of Canada. Those twenty-two persons met in this city and tried to come to an understanding as to what should be done to overcome the smuggling that then prevailed. Here is some information that was brought forth at that conference. 1 have a record of seizures made by United States customs officials for the two fiscal years ending June 30, 1928. In those two years there were 634 boats, 964 autos carrying liquor from boats on the United States side, 46,594 cases of beer, 6,644 barrels of beer and 16,360 cases of whisky confiscated. That is what the United States customs officials have a record of for those two years. But they also stated that this only represents from five to ten per cent of the total smuggling that was done during that two year period. If that is correct you will have to multiply those figures by about fifteen to twenty to get the total.
They also had on record at the conference the seizures made for the six month's period from July 1, to December 31, 1928, and they are very imposing indeed. There were 117 boats, 46,076 cases of beer, 4,576 cases of whisky, 375 autos in a total of 2,283 seizures. That is something of the history that we should go back to if we were to adopt this Bill No. 14.

It so happens that smuggling and hijacking and rum-running and bootlegging prosper under any government if given the opportunity to do so.
A chief argument used in favour of this bill is that it would increase the national revenue. Well, I think any of us here will agree that we need national revenue, but we are not all going to agree that we need it at any price. If we can get national revenue legitimately, without prejudicing the morals or the lives of our citizens, well and good. But if we cannot, if we are going to weigh upon the one side a few millions of national revenue and on the other side the morals and the lives of part of our citizenry then I think it will not take any of us very long to decide what the verdict should be. The condition that prevailed, especially along the Detroit river, and to a degree also along the Niagara river in the years preceding the passing of this legislation of 1930 is common knowledge. Gangsters, rum-runners, hijackers and bootleggers flourished like the proverbial green bay tree. They were waxing fat and growing rich. Not only were they taking chances with their own lives, but they were endangering the lives of many private citizens. We were informed at that time that the clearance to those vessels would be given in the daytime, and then they would run the river at night, at a time in the summer season when such river was just throbbing with all kinds of pleasure craft. There would be hundreds of small motor boats, row boats and pleasure seekers lining the Detroit, St. Clair and Niagara rivers at the time when the rum-runners would be shooting across with their cargoes. The result was that if the customs officials sought to intercept them and used firearms for that purpose they were endangering the lives of many innocent citizens. Indeed, we do not need to go far back to find that some innocent citizens were injured in that way.
Another important feature that developed in connection with the smuggling to the United States was the fact that there was a return smuggling of materials from the United States to Canada. It was proven that silks, cigarettes and other commodities were brought back into Canada by the smugglers who took the liquor from Canada to the United States, and our customs officials found it almost impossible to stop such traffic.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that if this legislation were before the public long enough for them to get seized of its importance and to realize its effect, we would have a flow of resolutions in here similar to what we had in the years

magazine, a newspaper or some other publication. The leader of the opposition gave two or three different reasons for his opposition to this measure, and I am not without some sympathy with the first of these reasons. The leader of the opposition stated that the original intention behind this legislation was to protect and maintain the integrity of officialdom within Canada, but that argument rather loses its force when we consider that the same thing goes on to-day. But it is covered up; instead of issuing permits for export to Detroit these permits are issued for export to St. Pierre, Miquelon, Jamaica, Cuba or some other place, though the officials know at the time the permits are issued that the liquor is on its way to the United States. So I do not see that this reason has any very great force. Undoubtedly when it is shipped to St. Pierre or some other destination the liquor is handled in the same way it was handled when it was exported to Detroit, and I think every official knows that when he signs these permits he is helping to get that liquor to the United States. There is another fact which is of some importance. When the liquor is shipped in this roundabout way it does not help swell the revenues of Canada. The liquor goes to the United States by a circuitous route, while Canada makes a noble gesture, pays dearly for the privilege and does not accomplish anything in the end.
The right hon. gentleman said very definitely that there never was any question of a quid pro quo, and that it was not intended that we should receive anything in return for our help in Mr. Hoover's noble experiment. Shortly after that, however, he took the attitude that this measure was passed in order to carry out the provisions of existing treaties with the United States. As I see it, there was only one reason for the adoption of this measure, and that was in order to assist the United States in maintaining the prohibition law. Those of us who have lived across from the United States for many years have seen the absolute farce, futility and failure of that method of trying to make people temperate, and surely to-day we should be prepared to listen to the voice of the greatest democracy in the world, which has definitely stated that the repeal of the prohibition act should be brought about. We did our part in the experiment; now the people of the United States have said they are through with prohibition and that they are going to enact such legislation as will
Liquor Export-Mr. Brown

permit the development of temperance by means of education. We cannot help them any longer.
The hon. member for KinTersley (Mr. Carmichael) referred to some of the abuses which undoubtedly existed previously. Does it necessarily follow that with proper regulation and supervision these abuses will develop again? The United States have said they desire the repeal of prohibition, so why should we go through the hypocrisy of sending liquor by the circuitous route which is followed at present? I am prepared to do my bit to see that they get the liquor they want; to see that they get good liquor and that they get it direct. Let our manufacturers and workmen benefit from the increased employment which will result, because we are in a position to secure a market which to-day is extremely difficult of access. I believe the country needs the revenue which will result from the export of liquor to the United States, and for all these reasons I am prepared to support the motion.

I cannot allow this motion to be voted upon without expressing my opinion in regard to it. The existing legislation was passed three years ago, in response to a very widespread demand on the part of the Canadian people, and by passing that legislation the government of the day recognized that the Canadian people were strongly in favour of that step being taken, not only in the interests of the United States but also because it was a duty we owed our own self respect.
One cannot help asking the hon. gentlemen who have supported this resolution the reason for all the hurry. If conditions in the United States are as they declare them to be what is the reason for all the haste? The hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) and the hon. member who seconded the resolution stated that the sentiment in the United States now is different from the sentiment which appeared to exist three years ago, and they said that Mr. Roosevelt's election, together with his promise to bring about the repeal of the eighteenth amendment, warrants us in repealing our own legislation. Well, it is not so perfectly certain that Mr. Roosevelt is going to be able to fulfil his promise. We have had abundant experience with men who have been elected because of great promises but who have not been able to fulfil those promises. It might very well be that Mr. Roosevelt will not be able to fulfil those promises. It must be pemembered that the system of government in

the United States is not the same as we have here. Mr. Roosevelt has only an indirect voice in legislation and before the eighteenth amendment can be officially repealed it will be necessary for three-quarters of the states to express themselves through their legislatures in favour of the repeal. I ask hon. gentlemen who are supporting this bill: What assurance can you give us that thirty-six out of the forty-eight states will vote for the repeal of the amendment? That in itself should be sufficient answer for the hon. member for Hamilton who is supporting this bill, but there seems to be another and if necessary a more conclusive argument to be offered.
The hon. member for Hamilton is a lawyer and lawyers are supposed to be well versed in the law and to be able to give an opinion as to its effect. As I recall the terms of the legislation it refers to any country into which the importation of liquor is forbidden, the United States not being specifically referred to. If this is true, the minute their proposed legislation becomes effective our legislation ceases to have any force. That seems to be a sound argument, so why the haste? Why cannot hon. gentlemen wait a little while?

Mr. Speaker, I shall not detain the house at great length but I wish to put myself on record in connection with this bill which is now before us. May I say that I am almost in complete agreement with the hon. member who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Brown). I have listened very carefully to the arguments advanced from this side of the house and whether or not hon. members like it I am bound to say that I have not heard a single argument which had any cogency or logic. The only complaint I have to make against the hon. member for Lisgar is that he has to a large extent covered the ground which I intended myself to cover.
The act which it is proposed to repeal is not expressly directed against or in favour of the United States, although it is perfectly true that the general principle it embodies was enacted into law because of circumstances existing and reasons connected with conditions in the United States. All that the act does, however, is to lay down a broad principle, that it shall be illegal in Canada to export to a country any goods the importation of which 53719-137
is by its law prohibited. That is a clear principle and it does not matter whether it refers to the United States or to any other country. It is a sound principle which has been recognized over and over again as being legitimate in the enactment of laws by countries, that is to say, that the legislation of a country shall make it unlawful for its subjects to make use of the country itself for the purpose of plotting and carrying out illegal operations in another country. We should not allow the citizens of this country to take active measures and perform overt acts directed intentionally and with our knowledge to the breach of the laws of a friendly state. If that principle is correct, and surely it is, what force can lie in any of the arguments for repeal which have been adduced from this side of the house?
Let nae review them for just a few minutes. It is said that we should repeal the act and draw our pen through the broad principle which the act enunciates, because we are receiving or have received no corresponding benefits from the United States. Have we passed legislation of this nature because of considerations coming to us from any other state? Surely the principle on which we have acted is one that is either right or wrong. The matter is not one of money, nor of weighing the pros and cons of consideration; it is the broad general principle I have laid down, namely, that no state can knowingly allow its citizens within its territory to plot a breach of the laws of a friendly state and to use its territory for the purpose of launching an attack against the laws of such state.

subtopic: PROPOSED REPEAL OF PROHIBITION OF LIQUOR EXPORT, ENACTED IN 1930
speechtext: Why should the United States allow the export of alcohol to this side without any convention preventing it?

subtopic: PROPOSED REPEAL OF PROHIBITION OF LIQUOR EXPORT, ENACTED IN 1930
speechtext:
I am not concerned with whether other states observe to the letter the principle that I have laid down. I do not think any hon. member can seriously question the accuracy of the statement that I have made. How then can the argument that in return for recognizing and observing this principle, we are not receiving any benefit from the United States, have any bearing on the question?
Then the argument has been advanced that there is a loss of revenue to Canada. If the principle be sound, surely that is not an argument against our observing it.
A third argument was used that our present act has in fact resulted in no benefit to the United States because that country has not effectually enforced its prohibition laws. What have we to do with that? That is the con-

Liquor Export-Mr. Bury

cern of the United States. That does not exonerate or relieve us from our responsibility; it does not make it right for us to countenance our own citizens in Canada plotting, planning, conniving and acting towards a breach of the laws of a friendly country.
Then there was a fourth argument, that payments have been taken by the United States authorities from violators of United States acts. The hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) stated that until he heard that argument, he was convinced of the cogency of the arguments advanced in favour of the act which it is now sought to repeal, but that a statement of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) that the United States federal authorities had been collecting money from violators of their country's law, effectually and neatly punctured all the force of the arguments which had been advanced and made him feel it was quite right then for us to connive at a breach of United States laws. I must say I am amazed at the hon. member for Labelle attaching any weight to that argument as an answer to the duty resting upon the Canadian government to see that its (citizens did not consciously and intentionally violate the laws of another friendly country.
Let me take another argument. It has been stated that there has come in United States sentiment a change which justifies the repeal of our present act. That also is quite immaterial. Whatever change there may be in United States sentiment, there is as yet no change in their law. We are dealing not with the nature of United States sentiment, but with breaches of United States law, and as long as their law remains what it is, that it shall be illegal to import liquor into their country, so long, whatever the sentiment of that country is or may become, we must observe that as being their law and honour it in our legislation. If we do anything else- there is no use blinking the fact or trying to hide the truth from ourselves-we are only dishonestly, hypocritically, for our own profit making use of a plea that has no legitimate force; we are dealing with a matter of change in United States sentiment of which we constitute ourselves the judges and are electing to act on a matter which is entirely outside our province. We are concerned with the law of the United States, and when the sentiment of the United States is sufficiently altered to take that law off the statute book or to change the constitution accordingly, it will be time enough for us to consider a repeal of our own law.

Indeed, may I point out that when the law of the United States is changed in this respect there will be no need to repeal this act. Our act states that what is illegal is the exportation from Canada of liquor into a country which prohibits its importation. The moment it has ceased to be the law of the United States that the importation of liquor is illegal and the moment such importation becomes legal, there will be no need to remove our present law from our statute book. As a matter of fact it should not be removed. As it stands it is the enunciation of a broad general principle which must remain true after the United States amend, if they ever do amend, their constitution so as to render legal the importation of liquor into their country.
It was stated-I do not know whether or not it was given as an argument for repeal- that vessels under a certain tonnage do not require clearance. What that has to do with the question, I cannot imagine. If you repeal this law it does not matter whether a vessel is over or under a certain tonnage, the illegality of importation is wiped out and vessels of all tonnages can take part in what is at present an illegal traffic.
The hon. member for East Essex (Mr. Morand) referred to the noble experiment of President Hoover. We are not concerned with that, nor with any controversy between Mr. Hoover and Mr. Roosevelt. We are concerned only with the law of the United States as it is to-day. Whoever is responsible for it; and whether it is going to foe changed or not, or whether prohibition is a noble or ignoble experiment, or whether dt is going to be a successful experiment or not, has nothing to do with the matter.
Other arguments were adduced that the officials of this country at the time they give a ship a clearance of liquor from Canada to a foreign port or perhaps to one of the British possessions, know in reality it is ultimately coming back to America. What has that to do with the case? The officials of Canada are there to enforce the law of this country and our law says that there shall be no export of liquor from Canada to the United States so long as by the laws of that country its importation is prohibited. My hon. friend is surely not serious in suggesting that if a cargo of liquor is consigned from some part of Canada to Bermuda, the Canadian official would have a right to say: This is not going to Bermuda at all; it is going to New York or some other United States port and that he would have a right to set himself up as a judge to say whether a cargo consigned to' a specific port was or was not going to that

Liquor Export-Miss Macphail
port. He is not concerned with that, he is concerned with seeing that no liquor goes from Canadian ports consigned to United States ports, and he is doing his duty when he does that. If, because of some gerrymandering at such foreign port to which the ' liquor goes, or on the high seas, the law is broken, that is not his concern.
I do not think there is anything else I can add, except this, in reference to some statements made by the right hon. leader of the opposition. Had I been in the house in 1930 I should have taken precisely the same attitude as the right hon. the present prime minister then took. I should have expressed wonder why so many years had elapsed before this legislation was put on the statute books. I have listened to the right hon. leader of the opposition excusing the dilatoriness of his government on two grounds:	First, that it
was necessary to wait until a body of public opinion had formed in Canada of sufficient volume to justify the government in putting this legislation on the statute books. Mr. Speaker, the volume of public opinion in Canada has got nothing to do with this particular principle. This is a principle that is recognized and has been recognized for years. The present act should have been put on the statute books years before 1930, and for a government simply to sit still and wait till the pressure of public opinion forces it to put a law on the statute books is merely to play the part of a leader who leads in the same manneT as a man leads a wheelbarrow downhill, who is dragged or impelled forward by the force of public opinion so that he cannot do anything else.
Nor am I concerned with such expressions of opinion as have been referred to by my hon. friend from Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael). I am not concerned with waiting to hear what my constituents say on this matter. The principle is clear; the principle is broad; the principle is sound; the principle is true, and nobody can question it. Still less germane and relevant were the remarks of the right hon. leader of the opposition when he sought to excuse the dilatoriness of his government in 1930, and the years prior thereto, in putting the present law on the statute books on the ground that there was not till then a sufficient body of public opinion in the United States in favour of prohibition. What have we got to do with the body of opinion in the United States? We are concerned with the proper attitude of Canada in respect of the recognition of the laws of friendly countries beside

For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I propose to vote against the bill if it comes to a vote.

Rather we support a principle because it is a principle, and whether it pays us or not should not influence our action at all. I do think that in this case the honour of Canada is at stake. speechtext:
The
house has become so sentimental over this matter that it is time someone injected a little business into our discussion. I am not an advocate for the liquor trade at all, and never have been, nor on the other hand am I a believer in the Volstead Act or prohibition. I endorse everything that the sponsor of this bill has said, although I do not go so far as to endorse the quotations from newspapers that he gave to the house. After hearing my hon. friend from the border city, the hon. member for West Essex (Mr. Robinson), I made up my mind that I would say something on this bill.
I consider that prohibition is a perfect farce, and too much of the time of this house has been lost in discussing it. It does not matter what governments did in the past. We are bere to legislate for the future, and we want to help the business world rather than kill it. That is what I am interested in most-the business of the country. There has been altogether too much interference with the old channels in which business has been done for [DOT]centuries. The less interference there is by governments the better, but all governments have interfered with people who are doing business in their own way legitimately, because this stuff was being sold legitimately, although I do not argue that it was landed legitimately. I would be the last to allow liquor to go from Canada into the United States if the people of the United States did not want it, but I have never been convinced that they did not want it, and I am not now. When this matter was before us in 1930 I noted from an American newspaper which I got from a friend of mine giving prices on every brand of Scotch, Irish and Canadian whiskey sold in the United States. It proved that they were buying and selling liquor openly in the United States, and I knew that myself. I have been in Pittsburgh, and I have seen them making and selling whiskey every quarter of a mile. They were selling it for Sl -25 a quart. I never drank any of it because I would be afraid to

touch it. A great many members on this side of the house share my view on this question. They do not believe too much in temperance, but they are afraid to vote any other way lest they might lose a vote. I come from a temperance riding, but that does not hinder me expressing my views.
As I said before, I am not advocating the entrance of goods into the United States against the wish of that country; I would not do so if I thought they were really sincere and did not want liquor to come in. The right hon. gentleman opposite, the ex-prime minister, said the hon. member for West Essex, who sponsors the bill, had given no good reasons why the past legislation should be repealed. On the contrary I believe he gave many good reasons. The bill which passed the house in 1930 accomplished nothing. It simply drove liquor through a circuitous route into the United States. We lost money; many a man who had invested in stocks in the liquor business lost large sums of money. The past government was always killing the business men. They must realize that there was no sense killing him because to-day they are reaping the benefits of their folly of years past. Many men who bought liquor stocks legally on the stock market lost large sums of money. Those men as well as other people should receive fair consideration.
What is the use of a law which cannot be enforced? The legislation of 1930 has never been enforced. There are too many laws already on the statute books of the provinces and those of this federal government which cannot be enforced. Those laws are proving a farce, and by putting more and more on our statute books we would only be turning the public against us everywhere. When laws are impossible of enforcement it is only mockery to have them on our statute books, especially when we know they cannot be enforced.
I do not know whether the right hon. gentleman opposite was sincere when in 1930 he brought in this bill. I think he was looking for a nice moral question upon which he could go to the country-but he did not succeed in what he was attempting. He could have brought down that legislation years before, but he chose to wait for the psychological moment to pull a nice stunt. But the people were wise, and he did not accomplish his purpose. The great trouble in this house is that people do not speak their own minds, but speak the minds of some other people. They are not sincere. As far as I am
