speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED REPEAL OF PROHIBITION OF LIQUOR EXPORT, ENACTED IN 1930
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was somewhat surprised that there should be any doubt concerning my position with respect to this legislation. I cannot but think that the experience of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) and others, as to the uncertainty of their own minds just before the past adjournment makes them suspicious of the opinions of others. We do not change our minds each minute; we are not prepared to support an agreement one minute and oppose it the next, just because somebody else does. I merely mention that, in passing, to the hon. member for Lisgar.
In 1930 I followed the then leader of the government, the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and, as strongly as it was possible for me to do, supported the legislation. I gave my reasons-not all of them. I still think there was a reason I might have given, a reason perhaps as powerful as any which could be advanced, namely, that I conceive it to be a principle of international law-true, it has been acted upon only in a limited number of cases-that where a friendly nation has knowledge of the fact that another nation has prohibited the importation into their country of commodities, it is a breach of good faith, of good neighbourliness and of international law, as I appreciate it, to aid, abet and succour the breach of that law.
There is one serious doubt, however, with respect to the application of it, which arises by reason of the fact that the late govern-

Liquor Export-Mr. Bemett
ment made a treaty with the United States of America. That treaty was made for Canada through its then minister of justice, the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) and on behalf of the United States through its secretary of state, Mr. Hughes. I have never been able to understand or appreciate -which does not in any sense indicate that the provision was not based upon sound ground-the reasons for the concluding portion of article II of that treaty. Article II says:
The high contracting parties agree that clearance from Canada or from the United States shall be denied to any vessel carrying cargo consisting of articles the importation of which into the territory of Canada or of the United States, as the case may be, is prohibited-
That is my appreciation of what should have been said, and in my view the article should have stopped there. But this is what follows:
-when it is evident from the tonnage, size and general character of the vessel, or the length of the voyage ar.d the perils or conditions of navigation attendant upon it, that the vessel will be unable to carry its cargo to the destination proposed in the application for clearance.
- It will be recalled that during the customs investigation of 1926-27, it was made apparent that ships cleared for ports which there was no possibility of their reaching. This article, for a reason to which I shall presently refer, provides that the prohibition of clearance shall be made effective only when it is apparent that the vessel is carrying such cargo, or when other circumstances indicate that the vessel will be unable to cany that cargo to the destination named in the application for clearance. There, you will observe, is a tacit recognition of the legality of clearances. It has always been difficult for me to understand why that tacit recognition of the legality of clearances was inserted in the treaty. The treaty was signed on the 6th of June, 1924, and I have never been able to understand, nor do I yet understand, why the article should not have ended at the word "prohibited," thus making it read:
The high contracting parties agree that clearance from Canada or from the United States shall be denied to any vessel carrying cargo consisting of articles the importation o-f which into the territory of Canada or of the United States, as the case may be, is prohibited.
But it will also be recalled that during the debate that took place in 1930 I presented to the house the correspondence and read extracts from the documents showing that an effort had been made by the United States 
to negotiate a treaty along those lines. That effort failed. It failed because no action was taken by the Dominion of Canada. Now we have this incontestable fact, that on the 6th of June, 1924, the Dominion of Canada signed a treaty with the United States that by implication, applying any rule that may be applied as to the construction of documents, gave to such a clearance, by its recognition, the colour of validity and legality, except it be a clearance for a vessel that came within the latter part of article II. As I say, that is the only difficulty I have with respect to this whole matter and the application of the principles of international law to which I shall presently refer.
I have always thought that the analogous case was the so-called Alabama case. It will be recalled that during the American civil war, complaint was made by the northern states that Great Britain had violated neutrality by permitting a ship built at the Cammell-Laird yards at Birkenhead to escape, after warning had been given by the representative of the northern states. She escaped in 1862 to Teneriffe, where she was fitted out with guns to prey upon the commerce of the northern states, as a result of which extensive losses were sustained and many vessels destroyed. The United States continued to complain; negotiations proceeded for several years. Finally, on the 8th of May, 1871, the parties entered into the treaty of Washington, which dealt with many questions in dispute between Great Britain and the United States. The then Prime Minister of Canada, Sir John A. Macdonald, was one of the commissioners and plenipotentiaries for Great Britain who signed that treaty.
In that treaty three rules were agreed upon which should govern in determining the validity of the claims of the United States for damages for loss of its commerce. These three rules I submit have application to a case such as this. They are as follows:
A neutral government is bound

First.-To use due diligence to prevent the fitting out, arming, or equipping within its jurisdiction of any vessel which it has reasonable ground to believe is intended to cruise or carry on war against a power with which it is at peace, and also to use like diligence to prevent the departure from its jurisdiction of any vessel intended to cruise or carry on war as above, such vessel having been specially adapted, in whole or in part, within such jurisdiction, to wrarlike use.
Secondly.-Not to permit or suffer either belligerent to make use of its ports or waters as the base of naval operations against the other, or for the purpose of the renewal or augmentation of military supplies or arms, or the recruitment of men.

Liquor Export-Mr. Bennett
Thirdly.-To exercise due diligence in its own ports and waters, and, as to all persons within its jurisdiction, to prevent any violations of the foregoing obligations and duties.
Although these principles were not adopted as rules of universal application in international law, these words appear in the treaty:
Her Britannic Majesty has commanded her High Commissioners and plenipotentiaries to declare that Her Majesty's government cannot assent to the foregoing rules as a statement of principles of international law which were in force at the time when the claims mentioned in article I arose, but that Her Majesty's government, in order to evince its desire of strengthening the friendly relations between the two countries and of making satisfactory provision for the future, agrees that, in deciding the questions between the two countries arising out of those claims, the arbitrators should assume that Her Majesty's government had undertaken to act upon the principles set forth in these rules.
Then follow these words:
And the high contracting parties agree to observe these rules as between themselves in future, and to bring them to the knowledge of other maritime powers and to invite them to accede to them.
It is perfectly true that these rules, which are now a part of international law as far as Great Britain and the Dominion of Canada and the rest of the British empire are concerned, applied only to the principles of neutrality when there was war between contending states. The state of civil war that existed between the southern and the northern states made it incumbent upon Great Britain to preserve neutrality. As a result of the escape of the Alabama and other ships Great Britain was called upon by the award of the arbitrators to pay fifteen and a half million dollars, which was distributed in part amongst those who had suffered losses.
My view has been that we have a similar case with respect to the countries that have passed prohibitory legislation with respect to any commodities if we give the sanction of this country by granting clearances into that country of such contraband commodities. The rules of blockade with respect to international law, the rules with respect to contraband of war, can obviously have no application in time of peace, but by analogy I submit it is fairly clear that liquor is a contraband of peace. I think I said that in this house in 1930, intoxicating liquor is contraband of peace. Why? Because the supreme legislature of the United States has declared that it shall not be imported into that country, and a prohibition exists against its importation. We too have passed prohibitory laws with respect to many commodities; you will find the names and descriptions in our customs legislation. My view is that wherever you have a prohibition of the importation into a country of that which thereby becomes contraband of peace, jt is a violation at least of those principles of friendly relationships that exist between peaceful countries to force or to aid or abet in the forcing of said prohibited goods or commodities into that country.
It is by that principle I stand. I oppose this bill because it is to my understanding a violation of the true principle that should govern the relations between friendly states. If in time of war two belligerents are entitled to demand from a neutral country the application of the rules that I have mentioned, it is equally true that in time of peace, where there is a prohibition that makes a commodity contraband of peace, the same rules should be applied. We should be astute enough to see that not only are we not partners, but that we do not aid or abet or assist or permit anything being done by our country that militates against the maintenance of friendly relations, by becoming parties, or partners if you will, or aiders or abettors, if you will, in or to a violation of the law of a friendly state. That in my judgment is the principle that governs. By the application of that principle this bill should not pass. The legislation that was passed in 1930 gave effect to that principle. It tardily gave effect to it, in my judgment, and the only difficulty I have ever had is with respect to article II of the treaty, which in itself is a tacit recognition of the validity and legality of a clearance except under conditions that do not apply in this case at all.
The desire on the part of many that legislation of this character no longer should be applicable if one of our friendly neighbours sees fit to pass legislation removing the prohibition is not pertinent to this discussion, for the simple reason that no such legislation has been passed. What is more, under the terms of the existing legislation-and the house will remember the discussion which took place in 1930-it will be recalled that if the prohibition of the friendly state against the importation of the commodity is removed, the right to grant clearances at once revives, because there is no legal prohibition and it is no longer a contraband of peace. In that case the clearances could be granted validly and legally, and no longer could the charge be made that the Dominion of Canada had aided, abetted, assisted or even connived, if you like, in the violation of the laws of a friendly state.

Liquor Export-Mr. Bennett
Without going into the matter at greater length it is on this ground that I am unable to support the motion. May I add that the only reason I did not think it desirable to participate in the debate at an earlier stage was that this is a private bill. Personally I have grave doubts as to the competency of a private member to introduce a bill of this character; I think I could show good reason for that statement, because in my judgment it conflicts with one of the rules of this house, but in any case the bill is here before us. I thought the right of every member freely to express his opinion with respect to a private bill thus introduced should be in no sense lessened by any observations which might be made by the leader of the government, because it might be supposed that he was speaking as such. Therefore I have listened to the observations of hon. members of the house both in opposition to and in support of the proposed bill which has for its object the repeal of the legislation of 1930. I oppose this bill even as I supported the bill of 1930. I supported that bill for the reasons I then gave and for the reason I ventured to express to-day, namely that this country cannot become a party to the passing of legislation which gives countenance to the export to a friendly country of that which is prohibited by that country as a contraband of peace.

subtopic: PROPOSED REPEAL OF PROHIBITION OF LIQUOR EXPORT, ENACTED IN 1930
speechtext:
I
much regret to have to admit that the position taken by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to my mind is technically correct. There is no doubt that the passing of this legislation in 1930 was intended to be a gesture of goodwill towards a friendly nation, and if that nation were still of the same mind there might be some force in that argument to-day. I opposed the bill in 1930 because I always have been opposed to anything in the nature of prohibitory legislation in this country or anywhere else. If the same condition existed to-day that existed then the argument of the right hon. Prime Minister might be sound, but as has been well said by the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell), the people of the United States of America have voted by a majority of more than 11,000,000 to repeal that prohibition law. We know that steps are being taken by the legislative bodies of the United States to bring about that repeal, but we also know that because of the defects of the American constitution in all probability it will be two or three years before that end is achieved. Then will it not be a gesture of friendship and goodwill on our part towards the United States to say; "We will help you when you cannot 
help yourself"? I contend that by voting for this resolution we will be doing far more to create goodwill between ourselves and our neighbour to the south than we will do by saying:	"We will wait until, with the
intricacies and complexities of your constitution, which we do not think is a free constitution, you get rid of this prohibition and at last show yourselves before the nations of the world as a free people."
Before taking my seat I cannot help but direct the attention of the house to something that amused me a great deal. I refer to the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) appealing to the Prime Minister to help him out of his difficulty. That shows the condition of mind and the state of panic in which our prohibitionist friends find themselves-and I suppose under the circumstances I might have the right to say "I told you so." I do hope, Mr. Speaker, that the legislation of 1930 will be repealed by a majority equal to that with which it was passed. I see my friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) smiling. He was one of that brave band of eleven who voted against this legislation, and I know he will be consistent and vote for the bill now before the house. I was reading over the remarks made in 1930 by the present Prime Minister, then the leader of the opposition, in which he twitted the former Minister of National Revenue on his vote at that time. I sincerely hope that on this occasion the Minister of Railways will not leave himself open to the reproach from this side of the house that the former Minister of National Revenue received on that occasion.

subtopic: PROPOSED REPEAL OF PROHIBITION OF LIQUOR EXPORT, ENACTED IN 1930
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one of the noble eleven who stood out in opposition to the act passed in 1930 prohibiting the export of liquor from this country to the United States, I deem it my duty at the present time to give my reasons for voting as I did upon that occasion.
I recall very well the speech delivered at that time by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), then minister of national revenue. He described a visit which he had made to the city of Detroit. After very careful observation he came to the conclusion that the government and the people of the United States were not sincere in their efforts to prohibit the importation of

Liquor Export-Mr. Maloney
liquor from this or any other country. He told us of having seen a boat loaded and unloaded with liquor under the eyes of the officers of the law of that great country. I felt at the time that we were being made nothing more or less than policemen to enforce the laws of a foreign country. I could not conceive it to be my duty to support such a bill, as I felt it was not our duty to enforce the laws of the United States of America. These are some of the reasons why I voted against the bill in 1930.
At that time the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), then leader of the government, made the statement that perhaps not more than two per cent of the spirits entering the United States illegally came from our country. It was a fact that a considerable quantity of alcohol and its allied products were being consumed by the people of the United States, but where did the other ninety-eight per cent come from? Part of it was home manufactured, but a large part came from foreign countries. I could not see where cutting off two per cent would have any considerable effect upon the people of that country, and I asked myself the question: Why Should the people of Italy, of France and of Great Britain be permitted to have their liquor released for export to the United States or any other country and a penalty be placed upon our doing the same thing?
I pictured to myself the loss of revenue which would occur. We had a vague idea of the quantity of liquor which was being exported from this country, but we knew' for a fact that at least $20,000,000 per year of good American cash was coming into this country as payment for the liquor that went out. It may have seemed sordid to look at the matter in that way, but the fact was that they were going to spend the money, so why should we not get our share when the money was good?
I do not believe that any hon. member who spoke this afternoon objected on moral grounds to the terms of the bill now before the house, nor was such the case in 1930. At that time the legislation was not framed for the purpose of uplifting the morals of the people of this country; it was put before this house as a political issue. I think the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) made that veiy clear this afternoon, and I need not elaborate. It was not a moral issue, it was an election issue. Even though it had been a moral issue, I was prepared to take the same action. As hon. gentlemen have mentioned this afternoon, many of us do not believe in prohibition of any kind. Prohibition means taking the people by the throat
and crushing them down; we believe in moderation, not in prohibition.
After hearing the arguments placed before the house this afternoon against this bill, I cannot feel that I was wrong in 1930. The arguments are based upon a treaty entered into some years ago between Great Britain and her dominions and the United States, a treaty which had to do with shipping and liquor. There was also a treaty entered into in 1924 between Canada and the United States dealing with the smuggling of all commodities. This treaty was considered lightly until suddenly in 1930, when an election was looming, the government felt it necessary to prohibit absolutely the shipment from Canada of anything contraband to the United States.
We have kept rigidly indeed our part of the treaty, but what have our neighbours to the south done? The government of that day passed an act binding us to prohibit the export of liquor from this country to the United States, but what did they get in return? Did they insist that the United States should control the export of contraband articles from that country to Canada? Not at all. The result is that while we are not allowed to export liquor to the United States, the United States is shipping into this country millions and millions of dollars' worth of contraband goods, consisting of silks, tobacco, cigarettes, and various other commodities. We have kept our faith; they have not kept theirs. We have been told to-day that a change of sentiment has taken place in the United States, and no man can deny that. The United States for several years have been labouring under a law which was not popular. Let us bring back to Canada the revenue which we have been denied for the last three years; a very conservative estimate of the amount we have lost by the passage of the act at present in force, is $60,030,000. Mr. THOMAS REID (New Westminster) moved the second reading of Bill No. 25, to amend the Penitentiary Act (eight hour day).
He said: Mr. Speaker, the main object of this bill is to reduce the working hours of the guards and officials of the penitentiaries, who are now working from eleven hours in the day to thirteen hours at night. It is proposed in the bill that their hours of duty be reduced so that they will be the same as those of all other civil servants, namely for the period of eight hours each day. Penitentiary guards and officials are the only class of public servants who are compelled to work more than eight hours a day. It is not necessary for me to point out that there is no more exacting work than that of guard or instructor in a penitentiary. They have always to be on their guard and to exercise the utmost vigilance in handling men confined to the penitentiary, some at least of whom are scheming to escape.
It has always seemed strange to me that the guards and other officials employed in penitentiaries should be compelled to work such long hours, especially when all other classes of employees are employed only eight hours a day. I ask hon. members to compare them with the police forces and members of fire departments throughout the country. It is my understanding also that in provincial prisons the guards are asked to work only an eight hour day, and I am informed further that in mental hospitals that is the duration of their daily duty. Throughout Canada however we have here institutions in which men are compelled to work an eleven hour period in the day and a thirteen hour period at night. It may be argued that throughout the month their daily average is not more than eight hours, but I suggest that is not a fair way of looking at it. The fact is that in a twenty-four hour period two men are asked to do the work of three. Where there is so much responsibility, where constant vigilance is required, where instructors and guards must be on the alert every moment they are on duty, it is not in the best interests of the country to compel them to work eleven or thirteen hour periods. They are dealing with men whose liberty has been taken away from them, and some of whom are continually plotting escape as is well known. Some men in penitentiaries fear neither law nor mankind.

Penitentiary Act
At this time it is not my intention to discuss generally the conduct of affairs in penitentiaries; that phase of the matter may be discussed later. The purpose of the bill, with the exception of section 2, is confined wholly and solely to the hours of duty during which officers shall work. The purpose of section 2 is to reduce from ten to eight the working hours of prisoners. On one occasion at least when I raised the question of hours of duty to which officials were subjected the Minister of Justice replied that the hours of labour of prisoners had some material bearing on the matter. It is with that in mind that the second clause in which the hours of labour of prisoners are reduced from ten to eight, has been added to the bill. I may add that the provision for a ten hour labour period now contained in that section is a relic of by-gone days and when people worked much longer hours than they do to-day. As a matter of fact at the present time no prisoners work a ten hour day; they work eight hours and very often less than that.
There is a provision in the bill whereby the warden or deputy warden, if necessity should arise, may direct that the prisoners work longer hours. I believe the bill as it now stands should commend itself to all hon. members, and I ask favourable consideration by the minister and the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, where practicable I am in favour of an eight hour day for all government employees. In our legislation concerning the eight hour day it will be found that the eight hour period now applies to almost all branches of the dominion public service, but there is in our law a saving clause under which any particular branch of the federal service may be excluded from the operation of the eight hour day provision. One of the branches of the public service which up to the present time has been excluded is the penitentiary service. Under the Penitentiary Act all convicts who are sent to penitentiaries are sent there to do hard labour; that is a provision of the act. Hard labour embraces within its definition a ten hour day.
In the bill before us I notice a proposal to reduoe the working hours of convicts to eight hours. The law has always contemplated ten hours as a proper day's work for convict labour. When one considers the proposal to reduoe hours of labour the question of the number of guards required for penitentiaries at once arises. I am informed by the departmental officials that with the exception of a single letter received from one guard, there have been no requests from the guards for
a reduction in their hours of duty. There have been many requests, however, by labour organizations asking that a reduction be made in respect of all members of staffs in our penitentiaries and particularly in respect of guards. I find also in the matter of guards that the Canadian penitentiaries are perhaps not as well staffed as prisons in other countries, notably in Great Britain and the United States. It may be that our staffs are a little limited in respect of the number of guards. In Great Britain I find that in the great prison of Dartmoor, where they had the serious revolt last spring, for 440 prisoners there was a staff of 96 guards, about one guard for every five prisoners. In the various prisons of the United States, while there is no uniform rule on the subject, the average is about one guard for every seven prisoners, while in the Canadian penitentiaries the average is approximately one guard for every ten prisoners. At the present time the number of guards employed in all penitentiaries of Canada is 598, but this has been increased within the last three months owing to disturbances which took place in three of the penitentiaries. At the time of the disturbance in the Kingston penitentiary there were 96 guards and 957 prisoners; at St. Vincent de Paul 115 guards and 1,115 prisoners; at Dorchester 47 guards and about 470 prisoners. The total number of prisoners in Canadian penitentiaries is in the neighbourhood of 5,000, including those at Piers Island, B.C., and the total number of guards at the present time is 598, so the proportion of one to ten is pretty fairly maintained. And that proportion has been maintained on the basis of a twelve or thirteen hour day on the part of these guards. It is quite true, as my hon. friend who moved the second reading of this bill has stated, that the average hours of work of a penitentiary guard throughout the whole year do not amount to eight hours per day, but that average is arrived at after computing certain leave and absences which the guard is permitted.
Seven days a week.

speechtext:
I have had a report compiled upon the subject, and I find the matter has been under examination in the Department of Justice on several occasions during recent years. The average has been taken in respect to certain guards from actual time sheets. Their average for seven months is 203 hours and 50 minutes of service each per month. During the seven months the guards in question had 39 days' annual leave, two statutory holidays and 32 days' sick leave. The officers are paid for sick leave when they have sick
Penitentiary Act
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He says;
The night staff would remain as at present, except for the alternation in the deputy warden and chief keeper visiting rounds. To assure full control it would be necessary to have an additional deputy warden or chief keeper. 1 think that it would be preferable to have an additional chief keeper; one assistant steward, one assistant engineer, one guard fireman, and three more keepers would also be necessary.
These are the higher paid officers of the staff. He goes on to say;
Only the guards taking over the duty from the night staff till the opening of the prison would report at 6 a.m., and would work from 6 a.m. to 8 a.m.; then at noon from 11.30 a.m. to 2 p.m., and from 5.30 p.m. until 10 p.m., thus making eight hours duty. The assistant chief keeper would relieve the deputy warden and the chief keeper two hours each during the day, and visiting rounds would require to be additional duty for this officer during the night.
He places the additional cost as far as the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary is concerned at the sum of $45,000 a year, including salaries and uniforms. The other wardens do not favour the change according to the records in the department. And they point out that the guards themselves have not asked for the change except in very few instances.
Now, guards who serve on night duty do, I believe, serve as long as thirteen hours. They tell me that it is not good policy to attempt to change guards during the night hours. As I pointed out a few minutes ago, if guards are to be changed more frequently, there will always ibe a certain amount of delay when the change takes place; there will be the checking over of the men, or, as they call it in the penitentiary, "the count;" the checking of the tools and other material which has been used by the preceding watch or preceding guard. All these things involve extra trouble, a certain amount of delay and a very substantial amount of expenditure in increased staff. I do not think that under present .conditions one would be warranted in proposing the additional expenditure in regard to penitentiaries of say a quarter of a million dollars for the purpose of introducing at this time the eight hour day system. I should like to see such a system introduced; I Shquld like to see eight hours made a day's labour throughout Canada in all federal departments if it were possible to do so, but I do not think it would prove to be a very workable system in the penitentiaries at the present time. Certainly the guards in penitentiaries have very responsible positions. This week I read in the report of Senate debates that it was suggested by a certain senator that guards should be in the nature of evangelists, missionaries -or teachers, who could improve the prisoners while they were

Penitentiary Act
serving their time. I can only say that if we introduced guards of this sort into our .penitentiaries, the guards themselves very soon would became convinced that they were misplaced.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, our penitentiaries contain the most serious type of criminals to be found in the country. Of course .there is a distinction between a prison and a penitentiary. For the most part the prisons of Canada are under provincial jurisdiction, while the penitentiaries are under the Dominion government. Unless a man is sentenced to a term of two years or .more, and unless he is a criminal of the .more serious type he is not sent to a penitentiary. During the .past few years, however-perhaps since the war-we in Canada and perhaps the people of other countries as we'll have been invaded by a class of criminal, not all Canadians but from other countries as well, of a .more .desperate type than we ever experienced before. Some attribute this condition to the motor car. We know that the motor car bandit and the hold-up man are much in evidence in Canada to-day. Bank hold-ups are of almost daily occurrence; there have been no less than four in Toronto within the last ten days. These bandits are armed and do not hesitate to use their arms should occasion arise. As a result we have in the penitentiaries of Canada a very large proportion of desperate criminals serving very long terms. Of necessity the guards in these penitentiaries must be strong and courageous; they must be men of intelligence and judgment, and .they must be men who can be depended upon in any emergency. They have a very hard, reckless crowd with which to deal. Many of the prisoners seem to be entirely regardless of what may become of them individually; of course many are life prisoners, and they seem to be entirely careless of what may be done to them. They are desperate, and like necessity desperation knows no law.
We must have carefully selected guards, therefore, and in the future we will endeavour to pay more attention than has .been .paid in the past to the selection of guards. The position of guard is an important one, and to a large extent it is a dangerous one. If the guards themselves objected, to the hours of labour I think perhaps the matter might receive more .consideration but, as I have stated, I have found in the records only one case where a guard suggested the eight hour day, although during the past six or eight years many labour organizations have pressed for it.
What I take to be the most formidable objection to changing the system at present, however, is the actual money required to make
the change. With existing conditions in Canada I would not feel warranted in asking for the expenditure of an additional quarter of a million dollars, which would be necessary to put this change into effect, and I do not know that the change would produce any better results than we have experienced to-day. I should like to increase the number of guards in some of the penitentiaries, and as a matter of fact since the recent outbreaks this has been done. We have increased the number of guards at Kingston from 96 to 154, at St. Vincent de Paul from 115 to 140, and at Dorchester from 47 to 54. The staffs in the other penitentiaries remain unchanged. This was thought to be a wise precaution having regard to the conditions which undoubtedly existed in those institutions.
It must be remembered that at the moment we are faced with another rather heavy expenditure. We must take care of from five hundred to six hundred Doukhobor prisoners who are held at Piers island on the Pacific coast. That prison has been especially constructed for the purpose of looking after these prisoners, who have been sentenced to terms of three years imprisonment. A staff of guards had to be procured, I think in the ratio of about one to twelve, and the increase in expenditure occasioned thereby has been very considerable.
Under these .circumstances I would not feel warranted in recommending the change proposed by this bill at the present time. I do not commit myself or anyone else in regard to future policy in this respect, though personally I strongly favour the eight hour day upon government work.
The minister stated that the increased cost would be about $250,000. I wonder if he cauld tell me just what percentage that is of the total cost of penitentiary services.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I could not answer that question unless I had the estimates before me. If my hon. friend will look at the penitentiary estimates he will find the total cost shown, and he .can make the calculation himself.

I am in favour of the principle of this bill, especially since this country is committed to the eight hour day, but it seems to me that as this bill is drawn it is quite useless. The establishment of the eight hour day would depend upon the request of the warden or deputy warden, and we have just heard that only one warden is in favour of the principle, so this would not appear to be of very much use.
My second point in regard to this bill is that the penitentiarv system is undergoing
Penitentiary Act

reorganization, and it would be hardly fair for parliament to pass a bill such as this without giving the new organization sufficient time to consider the matter. So far as I am concerned I think eight hours is quite long enough for a guard to be on duty, but I believe we should allow this reorganization to take place before we consider any measure such as the one now proposed.
The second section of the bill is rather humorous; at present I think public opinion is rather changing with regard to the position of the convict. I have nothing to say with regard to the first offender; I always have been in favour of showing him every possible consideration. On the other hand, however, the second offender, the repeater, should receive no favour so far as this country is concerned unless we want to find ourselves, with regard to our penitentiaries and the whole question of crime, in a position similar to that in which our neighbour to the south finds itself to-day. It would not mean anything if we were to say the convicts should work only eight hours a day. Every prisoner has to be in his cell before dark, and that means that at no time do they work eight hours at a time. Then the suggestion is made that they should not be asked to work on fast days or thanksgiving days. I wonder what sort of thanksgiving day would appeal to a man in penitentiary. I do not think he would consider that thanksgiving day as anything worth having. Clause 2 is absolutely humorous; indeed it is ridiculous, especially to those who understand the present day conditions in the penitentiaries.
While I shall vote for the principle of the bill, I think it would be much better if this house reserved its opinion until we see how the new organization was working out. If the guards at Kingston penitentiary have been increased from 88 or 90 to 140, it may be that the superintendent and the new warden will be in favour of this bill. I think it would be unfair for the house to express or press its opinion before the new organization can get under way and express its views.
Mr. ANGUS MadNNIS (Vancouver South):	Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a
few words in support of this bill. During my experience with labour movements throughout the past year I have always found that when a shorter working day is asked for it is argued that such is not possible because of working conditions and costs. However, it has always been found to work very well when put into effect, and I am sure the same thing would apply in this instance.
The minister says that these guards are charged with very responsible duties. I have

no doubt that he is correct, but he should realize that a man charged with very responsible duties should not be asked to carry on with those duties for thirteen hours at a time. When a man has carried on very responsible duties for eight hours, I think it is time he should be relieved. Those of us who perform duties which take our attention for some considerable time know that as the hours wear on we get irritable and those with whom we are associated feel the effects of the long hours we have been at work.
Previously whenever the eight hour day question has been brought before the house we have been met with the argument that this is a matter of provincial jurisdiction and that this government could not do anything. In the present instance the Dominion government has full jurisdiction and the only obstacle in the way is that of organization and cost. Even with the additional, cost, there would be some saving 'because of the fact that a certain number of men would be taken off the unemployed list. The minister stated also that the guards themselves did not want this. The guards at Westminster penitentiary or others speaking for them have approached me on this matter to ask my support. The guards did not want their names made known hecause they were afraid it might jeopardize their positions. I am glad to know that the minister is favourable to an eight hour day and that this would be put into effect if times were different, but I do not think conditions could be more favourable than at the present time. Two or three years ago times were fairly good in this country and yet no effort was made to reduce the hours. I would suggest that this is as good a time as any to make this very desirable change.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey):	Mr. Speaker, perhaps this is not the
time to go into the penal system of Canada in any detail, and I do not propose to do so at the moment. I have no objection at all to an eight hour day for the guards, but I do not think the working day of the inmates should be reduced to eight hours. Every-one knows that what the convict fears most is loneliness, he dreads being shut in a cell from the time he comes off work until the next morning. To add to that period of loneliness would be unnecessary and needless cruelty. I am hoping that some beneficial results will come out of the recent disturbances which have occurred and that lights will be put in the cells by which the prisoners can read. At the present time the lights provided make it almost impossible for the convict to read for any length of

Penitentiary Act
time. The statement is made that school teachers are provided and the prisoners have an opportunity of educating themselves. Those are just words without meaning. They have forty minutes immediately after they eat to attend the classes, the worst time possible to attempt to study. The blood supply cannot be in the stomach and the head at the same time.
May I be permitted to make the statement that in my opinion the recent disturbances were not due to certain prisoners who had been recently sent to the penitentiary. The government is to be congratulated in having communists in the penitentiaries on whom the blame for the disturbances can be placed. If the penal system of Canada had been reorganized according to the report of the royal commission which sat when Mr. Doherty was Minister of Justice there would not have been any disturbances. I should like to quote very briefly from the report of this commission which sat in 1914, as follows:
Speaking for themselves, the members of the committee would not before undertaking this investigation have believed that the penitentiary system could have been as needlessly cruel as it in fact is, and the absence of those features of the system which involve unnecessary mental or physical suffering would not to any of them make prison any the less abhorrent.
That is the commissioners speaking, not the convicts. This very excellent report was reinforced by another one in 1921 by a committee appointed to advise upon the supervision of petitentiary regulations. There was also a resolution moved by myself and adopted by the government but never acted upon. Since 1914 nothing has been done to bring the penitentiary system of Canada up to date.
Our present system is based upon revenge and not upon reform. I disagree altogether with the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) who stated that we owed nothing to the repeater. The repeater is the result of poor environment, unsound heredity and an inefficient penal system. If there are a great many repeaters, then without going any further I think we can say that something radical is wrong with the penal system. Punishment should never be in the nature of revenge, it should always be with the idea of reforming the individual. At all times the state should be above the thought of wreaking vengeance on the individual.
Let me repeat what I said in the beginning. It would be the most cruel thing possible to limit the penitentiary working day to eight hours, because in that case the prisoners would be locked in their cells much longer than they are now. If the intention is that
the number of guards be doubled or increased,
I have no particular objection. So far as lack of money is concerned, we can take what we are spending on cadet training or the non-permanent force or some other source of useless expenditure, and put it to this use ' if it is needed. But this only shows that parliament in 1919 went very far in enacting an exceptional piece of legislation.
I stated that the Minister of Justice was wrong in suggesting that all those who were asking for repeal of section 98 were extremists, belonged to special associations which were radical in their views. I said that every year I was a member of the government I attended interviews with the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada and other labour associations, at which the repeal of this section was urged. Those associations are far from being radical in their views. I have taken the trouble to look into the report of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada for every year during at least the last six or seven years. In every one of their reports and at every one of their annual meetings they protested against this section and passed resolutions asking parliament to repeal it. Let me call attention more particularly to the report of the meeting of last year, 1932, held in Hamilton. What they did with regard to this section will be found on pages 222 and 223. In 1931 the Trades and Labour Congress, under the presidency of Mr. Tom Moore, met at Vancouver and there reiterated their objections to this section, as will be found on pages 19 and 185. In 1930 they held a meeting in Regina, where again the same resolutions were passed, and it is to be noted that at every one of those meetings the congress rejected motions advocating extreme measures; motions, for instance, asking for the liberation of prisoners who had been convicted for having taken part in riots. I refer first to the case of Rex vs. Jones, reported in Canadian Criminal Cases, 1-932,, page 81, where the appeal court upheld a conviction under section 87 made in pursuance of riots which had taken place on account of unemployment and trouble in Alberta. This meeting was reported in The AVcxrker of May 16, 1931, as follows:
Starting by singing tbe "International," Die meeting was thrown open to free discussion, and one speaker after another condemned the

church as an opium vendor, demanded noncontributory unemployment insurance and urged the workers present to join the National Unemployed Workers' Association. The first speaker declared, "what we want is an international soviet union."
It might be well to quote from some of the songs which were sung or distributed at that meeting. The first is the International, which goes as follows:
Arise, ye prisoners of starvation,
Imagine, this is in Canada.
Arise, ye wretched of the earth.
One would almost think they were speaking of some downtrodden, European country forty or fifty years ago.
For justice thunders condemnation,
A better world's in birth.
We have heard a good deal about that in the last two months.
No more tradition's chains shall bind us,
Arise, ye slaves, no more in thrall,
The earth shall rise on new foundations,
We have been not, we shall be all.
When it is all over, it will be found that the institutions of Canada will continue to go along just as usual. The chorus runs like this:
'Tis the final conflict,
Let each stand in his place,
The international soviet Shall be the human race.
The international soviet will never wave its flag over this grand old Canada. The next song was The Red Flag, which runs as follows:
The workers' flag is deepest red,
And shrouded oft our martyred dead,
And ere their limbs grew stiff and cold, Their hearts blood dyed its every fold.
To hear this song, you would think that there was nothing but violence being carried on in this country. The chorus reads:
Then raise the scarlet banner high,
Within its shade we'll live and die,
The cowards flinch and traitors sneer,
We'll keep the red flag flying here.
As yet it has not been up and I do not think it ever will be. The next, song is the Red Army March. It runs as follows: Comrades, the bugles are sounding, Shoulder your arms for the fray,
Boldly we'll fight for our freedom,
Bravely we'll hew out a way.
Born in the ranks of the workers,
Whose toil scanty wage must suffice, Brotherhood, unity, freedom,
This is our fighting device.
This is the type of song sung at these meetings.
And in a church.

Yes, but, as I pointed
out earlier, the church had nothing to do with it.
During the recent municipal contest in Toronto, several candidates were contesting the ward in which I live and part of which I have the honour to represent here. An article in the Toronto Telegram of December 29, 1932, refers to three of these candidates as follows:
Three of the candidates, members of the United Front Party and endorsed by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and selfavowed socialists, were the speakers most popular of the evening.
Mr. Speaker-

If the hon. member
wishes to do me justice he will remain in his seat and allow me to finish my remarks.
Mr. Speaker-
Sit down.

One of the candidates
was asked the following question:
Why is all the world in such a bad state of affairs?
And his reply was:
Because capitalism is in the saddle. We will have a revolution here as in Russia (I did not want to name Russia but I must), but I think it will come in a different way.
At many of those meetings in Toronto where these candidates were speaking, they were supported by groups of avowed socialists who, after these candidates had made their speeches, prevented other candidates for the city council or the Board of Control of Toronto, who wished to discuss the issues of the day, from speaking. In other words, the very advocates of free speech prevented free speech on many platforms during the municipal election in Toronto.
I should like to read what His Grace Archbishop McNeil says with reference to clean speech. His Grace, as reported in the Toronto Globe of June 22, 1931, spoke as follows:
The message given the Holy Name Society on Sunday by His Grace Archbishop McNeil is one which should cause people of all denominations to think. "If ever there was need for promoting reverence," be said, "it is in our day. To-day wide-spreading organizations exist in Canada, the United States and England to encourage atheism. There are even schools of atheism in this country. And the largest country in Europe has adopted atheism as its public policy."
It seems to be a fact that the forces operating against the spirit of reverence are more active and determined than those promoting it.

Criminal Code-Unlawful Associations
There are such organizations as the archbishop referred to, including the communistic schools, directly interested in wrecking the bulwarks of spiritual thought by spoken and written speech and evil example. In addition there is the insidious campaign of those who would give rein to atheistic doctrine in the name of "free speech." The former are conducting the "drive"; the latter is breaking down resistance. Where is the defence organization that has at its back the might of right, "the faith of the fathers," and the knowledge of a righteous cause?
I want to close just with this:	I am in
accord with maintaining on the statute book section 98 of the criminal code, and I shall support the amendment moved by the minister of justice. While I have been in the house I have heard those who assume that they represent labour, speak on many occasions. I have been associated with labour for twenty-five years and I yield to no one as regards the rights of the working man. I am convinced that organized labour in this country and in the United States deserves a great deal of credit for what it has done and what it proposes to do in the way of alleviating the condition of the working man, and on every occasion that organized labour advocates something for the betterment of the working man, I shall support it if I believe it is wise and just. Organized labour has been quoted as being in favour of the repeal of section 98. Let me say that organized labour is opposed with all its might to the preaching of violence and armed upheaval, because labour men would be the first to suffer and would suffer longest and hardest as a result of any armed upheaval. I would not be so much opposed to agitations of this kind if, when parades were organized and marshalled to bring about violence and armed uprisings, the paraders would seize the leaders who led them astray and would march them at the head of the procession, so that those leaders would be the first to suffer from the advocacy of violence and armed upheaval.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey): Mr. Speaker, it was my privilege a week ago to-morrow night to address a large congregation in Donlands church which is near the McGregor school in East York. I was invited by the Reverend Mr. Irwin, the pastor of the church, to give an address, I was introduced by Doctor Salem Bland.
Oh, oh!

I said there that I respected my colleagues in the house, but I am afraid, after the laughter at the mention of Doctor Bland's name, I shall have difficulty in doing so in future. As I said, I was intro-

duced by Doctor Salem Bland. I made practically the same speech as I made the following afternoon at McGregor school. The school, I may say, was crowded. I congratulated the school board in allowing, though I could never understand why it should be a case of allowing, the taxpayers in that school section to use the auditorium for public meetings and discussions. The minister of Donlands church, and the East York Workers' Association, almost all of whom were unemployed, could have selected their own member to address them. I did not ask them to invite me. Possibly their own member had better do some heart-searching to find out why he was not asked. I do not know why he was not.
As regards the subject to which the Mail and Empire was referring when I was reported to have said that there was less freedom of speech in Canada than anywhere else, the question I was discussing was freedom of action of elected members in the House of Commons, and I said that in the British House of Commons there was much greater freedom and that when a cabinet minister was not pleased with the action of his government, and when the action taken by his government was contrary to his personal convictions, he asserted his position as an indivdual, was true to his convictions and showed this by resigning from the cabinet, something that practically never happened in this country. I went on to say that what I believe constitutes one of the real difficulties of government in Canada is the slavish adherence in this house to parties. I said-and am afraid I cannot say it again-that I respected my colleagues in the House of Commons and that I believed if they were free individuals, free first to think, then to discuss and finally to vote on the merits of questions as they arose in this chamber, we would have very much better legislation than we now have and we would have avoided some of the great difficulties into which we have fallen. I still say that, and if the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. MacNicol), who has just spoken, means that in our speeches we must defend everything as it is, may I say that I do not intend to do so. It is a long time since I decided that the upper house was of very little use to Canada. The hon. member who has just resumed his seat may disagree with me. That is his business, but I do not propose he shall tell me what I shall think, and for the hon. member to try to link up, as he did quite definitely in his speech, those of us who go out to speak in school houses, churches and public halls, on the economic

Criminal Code-Unlawful Associations
condition and the need of constitutional reform-radical and fundamental, but constitutional-with communists, that just brands him for the excellent Tory he is. We are not communists, and I may say that the heckling that we receive comes from the communists who hate the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), myself and others associated with us more than they do anybody else, because we, by striving to bring about reforms constitutionally, stand between the communists and the violence they desire. The people who are aiding the communists most are the very ones who are afraid of them, and who will not consider any changes at all, but insist upon retaining such repressive measures as section 98 of the criminal code. They are the very ones who are helping, as I said in this house the other day, to bring about the thing they fear.
I am Canadian born, and I love Canada as much as any member who sits on the government side. My record of service in this country is as clean as that of any member in any part of this house, and I do not propose any longer to sit here and allow people to put into our mouths things that we have never said and attribute to us motives that we have never had. This business of continually trying to tie us up with Moscow is ridiculous; it is nonsense. It is a regular trick of the Conservative party. I remember when the Liberals were in power how the Conservatives were always saying that the fiscal policy of the Liberal government was dictated from Washington. Now if the financial policy of this government is not dictated by Wall street, New York, I should like to know who is dictating it. The Conservatives are always trying to tie up those opposed to them with dictation from some place outside of this country. I myself and the members of the United Farmers of Alberta and the Labour group in this house are Canadians. We are not tied up with Moscow, and never have been. We are taking no orders and no money from Moscow. May I say to the hon. member for Toronto Northwest that we are striving by constitutional methods, by the exercise of our intelligence, which thank God we possess-
[DOT]. Mr, MacNICOL:	You will never get any
money from me if you advocate that kind of stuff.
I would not want your money.
Then why mention it?

I did not; I did not
know the hon. member had any money. We
are striving by the exercise of our intelligence to bring about by constitutional methods the very reforms that must come. You cannot stop reform. You can try. You can stupidly stand in the path of progress and do all you can to stop it, but all you can succeed in doing is to dam the thing back until it gets beyond control and then causes the very upheavals and difficulties which we all deplore and which none of us want. I hope we shall not again hear such statements as those made by the hon. member for Toronto Northwest. I have no objection to the government members and the Liberal members fighting us on the merits of any question, but to intimate, as the last speaker did all through his speech, that we are closely associated with communists in this country is simply laughable, and may I add that I think the hon. member is not doing himself or his party any good. The people of Canada know that the Conservative party has no corner on Canadian-ism, that it has no corner on loyalty to this country, that it has no comer on a desire to serve even though it means sacrifice, and it is about time the Conservative party realized that. They have waved the flag and prostituted patriotism as no other group in Canada ever has done-we have heard it until we are sick of it-and when the flag won't do they take the Bible and wrap their policies in both, hoping the people will then stomach them, and it is sometimes all they can do. We have listened to altogether too much of that sort of thing.
I am going next week-end to Toronto to address an audience in a school auditorium, having been invited by a man who has about ten letters after his name, whatever they stand for, and who is as good a citizen I presume as the member who has just sat down, and if you care to hear what I have to say, come if you want to. But do not quote a paper like the Mail and Empire, one of the most partisan papers in Toronto, and one that is now spending a great deal of money to try to increase its subscription list. I suppose as the number of Conservatives in the country declines, so do the subscriptions of the Mail and Empire.
I do not very often protest so heatedly, but this thing has gone so far that even respectable members of the house like the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) and the hon. member for West York (Mr. Lawson) are getting up and seriously saying these things which men of their intelligence must know are not true. They are intelligent men; I will say that for them. Instead of abuse, why not meet the issue on its merits? I

Criminal Code-Unlawful Associations
think that this game of misrepresentation has been played too long in Canada, and I do not think that it will deceive the people again. That is all I care to say at the moment.

I had not intended to take part in this debate, but some of us back benchers have been so frequently charged with being afraid to get up and express our views (that I feel I must say a few words in regard to section 98 of the criminal code.
I want to inform the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) that it was my .privilege last summer on the twelfth of July to introduce a resolution approving of section 98. I suppose I shall be condemned as a loyalist for having introduced it on the twelfth of July, but I do not apologize for that. The resolution was presented at a picnic attended by at least three thousand people in the constituency of Rosetown, and most of them were farmers. The resolution endorsed the action of the government in retaining section 98 of the criminal code, and recommended that under present circumstances the section should be retained. That resolution was passed unanimously, with not a dissentient voice, and as I said, a large proportion of the people present were farmers. We are passing through a severe depression, and it is necessary that we meet in an orderly and. constitutional way, difficulties as they arise. I think that that is the attitude of the farmers not only of Rosetown constituency but of western Canada. I believe that if hon. members of the party in the far corner of the house would do a little more to help solve the problems of the farmers of western Canada and come to their relief instead of talking so much about the elimination of section 98 from the criminal code, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation might receive better support than it is getting. I am convinced that our friends in the far corner are doing themselves no good in western Canada.
I was in the court house at Kingston yesterday when four of the convicts from Portsmouth penitentiary were brought in for examination, and I notice that the Ottawa Journal of this evening has this to say:
Three more convicts of Portsmouth penitentiary, making 18 in all who have been sent up for trial, were committed by Magistrate J. M. Farrell in county police court to-day. All are charged in connection with the penitentiary riots of last October.
Further hearings were adjourned to-day until Monday. Prominent in the trio facing trial to-day was Albert Dorland, whose claim of being "framed" by Toronto police brought police commissioners from that city two weeks ago to interview him. Do-rland is serving a five-year term for possession of firearms.
r.Miss Macphail.]
Murray Kirkland, who figured in a sensational bank robbery in North Toronto three years ago, when $10,000 was dropped by the bandits and recovered by a child, was the second committed.
The third was Robert Spinks, sentenced in Sarnia in 1927 to a 20-year term for a serious offence.
The caretaker of the court house informed me that three of the men were born in Russia, and I presume from the names that it was these three Russians who were committed for trial.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) the other night, in addressing the house, said that if ever there was a time when we should retain section 98 in the criminal code, that time is now. As a member from western Canada I feel I am voicing accurately the sentiments of people in that part of Canada. It is alarming to me to hear some hon. members, and especially the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail), who unfortunately has left the chamber, state that some of the back benchers dare not say a word for themselves. Last fall we were subjected to the same criticism. We came to parliament last fall to ratify treaties, and some hon. members made an effort to ecnomize and not to take up too much time in debate. That has been my attitude since my appearance in this House of Commons. I believe the pros and cons on each subject are placed fully before this chamber, and for that reason as a new member I hesitate to make lengthy statements. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre must be familiar with the resolution passed last July 12, because I met him on the same ground a few years ago. When I tell him it was passed at Crystal Beach, Saskatchewan, he will be familiar with part of the country to which I refer.
I do not wish to take up much of the time of the house, but I should like to add that the people in my part of the country are behind the government one hundred per cent, and we contend that section 98 should remain in the criminal code. Of course we have our troubles in that section of the country. I could mention other things I should like to have done, but at a later point in the session I shall outline them. I could not help but resent the challenges of the hon. member for Southeast Grey when she referred to the loyalty of our people. I have always boasted that I was of Empire Loyalist stock. I am proud to think that there were people who had the courage to come into this country, cut away the bush, build shanties, and, as their next move, put up little churches. That fairly well describes the type of people who

Criminal Code-Unlawful Associations
came out here, and it is characteristic still of the people of tihie west. I can only say that heredity must have something to do with the spirit of our people, and I could not sit in my seat in this House of Commons and hear criticism levelled at them of the kind that has been made to-day.
On December 28, a gentleman from Regina, a Mr. Coldwell, came to our constituency, and on that occasion he spoke in terms similar to those employed to-night by the faon. member for Southeast Grey. He intimated that last August he had occasion to travel through British Columbia, and that while his train was stopped at Banff he got out and ascended a certain hill. At that particular moment a short freight train was passing through a tunnel and as it emerged from the tunnel Mr. Coldwell counted 206 transients riding on it. When he had completed his remarks I got on the platform and asked this question: "Would you believe, sir, that those 206 men, or most of them, had probably got on that train before the harvest started; in other words, that they wanted to get out of our country before the work started?" I told him to go on to Rose-town and he would learn from the people of that place that when the harvest started men had jumped on a freight train and migrated to British Columbia. I am not suggesting that all labouring men are of that type, but I do want to say in all fairness that I cannot believe that labour and farmers can harmonize; they cannot do it.
Some years ago I employed some men on my farm who sat in their tents at nights and sang hymns out of red-backed hymn books. I would pass by their tents after the day's work was over, and after I as their employer had done as big a day's work as any of them. I would hear them saying in effect: "Isn't that farmer an awful fool?"-calling me by name -"Isn't he eager to get rich? Look at the way he works his wife to feed us." Then they would say: "Some day everything will be equal; we will all get the same. Some day we will visit his farm and take away his pigs and his steers." At that time I was paying some of those men as high as $7 a day. What happened? I was forced to buy combines because their wages were so high. I can remember one occasion when some of the men I had hired put a coil of soft wire in a stook, undoubtedly for the purpose of ruining some of my machinery.
Some such men are still travelling up and down this country on trains. Even to-day they try to hold us up for $5 a day when we are receiving only 25 cents a bushel for our wheat. I want hon. members to realize I am in sympathy with the labouring man. I know labourers are not all of the type I have described, but there is a certain element which would like very much to rule the country, and their attitude has been apparent for some years.
May I say again that while I have not spoken on many occasions in the house, certainly nobody has been restricting me. In this particular I believe I am speaking the minds of all back benchers. I am not anxious to have my name in Hansard; I am not looking for publicity. The people of my constituency were good enough to elect me to this House of Commons, and I am not worried about the future. I will stick to the people of Rose-town constituency who still have faith in me, whether or not I have my name in Hansard every day, or frequently take up several hours of the time of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I am not greatly interested in comic opeTa revolutionaries or would-be comic opera dictators. I intend to present what I consider to be a purely trade unionist viewpoint concerning the bill before this house. By heritage and conviction I am a trade unionist. Since my return from the war I have attended most of the conventions of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. Without equivocation I wish to state clearly that I am absolutely opposed to the philosophy and tactics of communism. I believe I can agree with some hon. members when they state that communism is absolutely foreign to the mental make-up of Canadians and the Anglo-Saxon people. I have always taken the stand that no person has a right to enter this or any other country where democratic institutions exist and preach the forceful overthrow of those institutions. It is pure logic that those democratic institutions should protect themselves, and I believe my views in this connection cannot well be controverted.
I listened with a great deal of attention to the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie). It is my view that the present government is responsible more than any other force for the existence of the communist party in Canada. I make this statement because of my practical experience, and because of my knowledge of the methods used by the communist party in Canada in their effort to destroy the trade union movement. Men active in the labour movement have possibly received more criticism, I suppose, than the members of the government from that direction. They call us labour fakers and apply to us all the adjectives they so commonly use in respect to the responsible labour leaders

Criminal Code-Unlawful Associations
not only in this country but in every country where the communist organization functions. I want to point out, in a very practical way, that the position taken by the government in declaring the communist party an unlawful organization has driven it underground; they have a different name almost every week for their different local organizations, and in my judgment this supports the contention of the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) that in the final analysis the best attitude to adopt is absolute freedom of speech. I say that from my own practical observation. Last May day in Hamilton these chaps wanted to hold a meeting in one of the large parks. They were refused permission. Everyone was on hand to see the fun; there were about fifteen thousand people. The firemen turned out and laid the hose in case of emergency. Someone threw a brick at one of the firemen; the water started, and the fire and police departments made enemies of those innocent bystanders.
Not so long ago when I was in Detroit I saw an anarchist holding forth in what I think they call the grand circus there. He was raising eain about everything in general-the mayor of the city, the responsible government officials in the state and federal assemblies. About a thousand people were listening. So I say, as a result of my practical experience in contact with different individuals representing various viewpoints both on the left and the right in the labour movement of this country, that it is far better to have complete freedom of speech. Apart from the principle I think it is the most practical thing to do.
We of the trade union movement have taken the attitude that we are not interested in the expression of opinion or even the guarantees of members of parliament in this regard. They are not the ones who sit and interpret the law. We cannot rest content even with a guarantee from the Minister of Justice. Arising out of our struggle for existence, almost within the lifetime of some in this chamber men were deported simply for belonging to a trade union. The trade union movement has gone through a continuous struggle to maintain its existence as an instrument in the upbuilding of the social status of the great bulk of the working people that make up the industrial life of this country and of Great Britain where the movement had its inception.
The ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) quoted from the record of the Trades and Labour Congress at its last convention in the city of Hamilton. A resolution passed by that

body called for the repeal of section 98 of the criminal code. I was a member of a delegation which on January 27, in this city presented a brief through Mr. Moore, the president of the congress, stating that in their opinion section 98 of the criminal code is too wide in its application and unduly restricts freedom of speech. In 1920 the congress was so alarmed at the implications of this section that they went to the trouble of getting legal opinion. That position was unanimously adopted by the congress in session in Windsor, Ontario, on September 30, 1920. I would like to read this into the record, because it. gives clearly the attitude of the responsible trade union movement of this country towards this particular section. It says:
As to conspiracy itself, Wright in his book on Criminal Conspiracies, says: "No intelligible definition of conspiracy has yet been established.'' The Hon. Edward Blake, in 1890, while discussing, in the House of Commons, the subject of the protection of trade unions from prosecution as conspiracies in restraint of trade, called it the "obnoxious law of conspiracy."
A conspiracy is an agreement to do an unlawful act, or to do a lawful act in an unlawful way.
Before closing the subject, I should direct your attention to the amendments of 1919. I have already referred to the repeal of the provision declaring what was not to be deemed seditious. There has been added a section (97b) as follows:
"Any person who prints, publishes, edits, issues, circulates, sells, or offers for sale .or distribution any book, newspaper, periodical, pamphlet, picture, circular, card, letter, writing, print, publication or document of any kind, in which is taught, advocated, advised or defended, or who shall in any manner teach, advocate, or advise or defend the use, without authority of law, or force, violence, terrorism, or physical injury to person or property, or threat of such injury, as a means of accomplishing any governmental, industrial or economic change, or otherwise, shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for not more than twenty years."
Further subsections deal with the circulation of such enumerated documents by mail and with the importation of them. While the word "seditious" does not appear in the section, the side note reads:	"publishing, etc., seditious
books, etc."
The penalty for speaking seditious words was, under section 134. limited to two years. The two years limitation has been done away with and the imprisonment may now be as high as twenty years.
I add. also, the new section with respect to "unlawful association."
"Any association, organization, society or corporation, whose professed purpose or one of whose purposes is to bring about any governmental, industrial or economic change within Canada by use of force, violence or physical injury to person or property, or by threats of such injury, or which teaches, advocates, advisee or defends the use of force, violence, terrorism or physical injury to person or property,

World Economic Conference
or threats of such injury, in order to accomplish such change, or for any other purpose, or which shall by any means prosecute or pursue such purpose or professed purpose, or shall so teach, advocate, advise or defend, shall be an unlawful associ ation."
Provision is then made for seizing the property of unlawful associations and for prosecuting its officers and members, and punishment is provided for wearing its badges etc.
The attention of the congress should be directed to the words "force" and "terrorism," in the above sections, coupled as they are with the words "industrial or economic change."
The use of these words leaves the door wide open for the prosecution of every trade union in Canada. If "force" is intended to mean "physical force" it should be so stated.

In the votes
and proceedings of February 15 there is an item at the bottom of page 227 under the heading "Erratum", with regard to adjustment of war claims. This item carried in committee on the fourteenth. My recollection is that in the course of discussion on the item I asked the Minister of National Defence where we could get the information we desired with respect to an appropriation of $500,000 in the previous year which was not to be renewed. The minister replied that we could obtain it from the Secretary of State when we came to his estimates, but there is no place in the estimates of the Secretary of State, so far as I can see, where we could bring up that item. I should like to ask the Prime Minister if it can be understood that we may return to that item for the purpose of getting any information we wish if we allow this matter to go as having been passed. Otherwise we shall have to get the information in some other way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I was in the chamber
when the incident to which the right hon. gentleman refers took place, and I recall the reply of the Minister of National Defence to the question asked by the right hon. gentleman. It is true that the Minister of National Defence would not be in a position to deal with the particulars of that item, which would fall within the duties of the Secretary of State. If it will suit the convenience of the right hon. gentleman I will arrange that when the estimates of the Secretary of State are under consideration this item will be discussed. Will that be satisfactory?
I wished to make sure that we would have that opportunity, because I could not find any place where this matter could be taken up under the estimates of the Secretary of State.
